docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Societal Analytics Lab (VU Amsterdam) runs a small infrastructure for its research: a login service, servers for the tools lab members use, and servers for the research software the lab develops (AmCAT, AnnoTinder). This site describes how that infrastructure is set up and secured, and how our software handles logins. It is written for lab members, for VU IT, and for other research groups with similar needs.

docs.title: Two kinds of servers
docs.text:
• Physical servers on VU premises: the lab server and the database server. Used for work that needs dedicated hardware or a lot of storage.
  • Virtual machines (VMs) from VU SciCloud, the VU's research cloud (one.labs.vu.nl, see SciCloud). Used for services that are better off on a server of their own: the login service, and some of the lab's services.

Lab services run on the lab server or on a service VM, whichever suits the service best. An overview of the services: Hosted services.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication: where should it live?
docs.text:
Evaluation

This page is the evaluation behind our choice to keep 2FA at the OIDC provider (November 2026). The decision and its reasons are on the Decisions page. Where this page mentions our shared provider for other teams: that was dropped later. Teams without a provider with 2FA can now use weaker security settings for teaching servers.

All our software requires a second factor (2FA, MFA) for sensitive actions (see the Authentication standard). This page discusses which component provides that second factor: the OIDC provider (option A), or a component of our own (option B). It explains the relevant concepts, lists the pros and cons of both options, and ends with a recommendation.

This page is about AmCAT and AnnoTinder, including when other teams host them. The lab's own login service is described on the Keycloak VM page.

docs.title: Authentication factors
docs.text:
A factor is a type of proof that you are who you claim to be: something you know (password), something you have (phone, security key, access to an inbox), or something you are (fingerprint, usually used to unlock a device). Two-factor authentication means that a login requires two different types of proof, so that stealing one is not enough.

Two things are easy to overlook:

  • Email is a factor. Logging in via an email link, or via an account whose password can be reset by email, proves possession of the inbox. A login without 2FA is therefore usually one factor, no matter how many screens it has.
  • A factor that can be recovered by email is not a second factor. If a lost authenticator app can be replaced by clicking a link in your inbox, an attacker with access to the inbox can do the same. Real 2FA needs a recovery route that is stronger than email: recovery codes, a second registered device, or a person (admin, helpdesk) who verifies your identity. This is true for both options; they differ in who handles recovery.

docs.title: Second factor types
docs.text: Type Notes Passkeys / WebAuthn (device biometrics, security keys) Bound to the website's domain, so they can't be phished on a look-alike page. The strongest common option. TOTP (authenticator apps, 6-digit codes) Widely supported, but can be phished: a fake login page can ask for the code and use it immediately. SMS Better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM swapping.

docs.title: OIDC claims
docs.text:
An OIDC provider returns an ID token with claims about the login. The ones that matter here:

Claim Meaning iss + sub The provider (issuer) and the user at that provider. Together they are the user's identity. email + email_verified The email address, and whether the provider confirms the user owns it. auth_time When the user last actually authenticated (not when the token was issued). Used to check freshness. amr Authentication methods used, such as pwd, otp, mfa. Standardized names exist, but providers decide which values they send and when. acr The level of the login, e.g. a level-of-assurance URI. Institutional federations (including SURFconext) often signal 2FA through acr instead of amr.

docs.title: Step-up and freshness
docs.text: Step-up authentication means asking an already logged-in user for a fresh second factor before a sensitive action, such as creating an API key or changing roles. With an OIDC provider, the server sends the user back to the provider with max_age (re-authenticate if the last login is older than N seconds), and then checks auth_time and the 2FA claim in the new token itself. The server must check this itself, because providers don't always enforce what was requested. For instance, Keycloak had a vulnerability (CVE-2026-97176) where a token could be issued at a lower level than requested.

docs.title: Threats
docs.text: Threat Description T1. Stolen password or inbox The most common attack. Any real 2FA stops it. T2. Email reassignment Old email addresses get reassigned, especially institutional ones. Our safeguards exist for this. T3. Compromised or misconfigured provider A breached provider, a careless admin, or weak account recovery at the provider. The provider can then issue valid tokens for any user. T4. Phishing A fake login page captures credentials and one-time codes. T5. Lockout A user loses their second factor. Not an attack, but recovery procedures are a common attack surface themselves.

docs.title: Option A: the OIDC provider handles 2FA
docs.text:
How it works

  • The OIDC provider requires 2FA, and signals it in the ID token. Which claim counts as 2FA is configured per deployment with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM (e.g. amr containing mfa, or a specific acr value).
  • For sensitive actions, the server checks the claim and auth_time, and redirects to the provider with max_age if the login is too old.
  • Teams without a suitable provider can use our shared OIDC provider (the idp realm of our Keycloak, which signals 2FA in amr) for servers without sensitive data.
Pros Cons The standard pattern. Auditors, university IT and other developers recognize it immediately. The 2FA signal differs per provider. Each provider needs to be checked and configured (see Provider support). No 2FA code in our software. Enrollment, factor storage, phishing-resistance and rate limiting are the provider's job. Teams need a provider with 2FA. Free and simple providers often lack it. Our shared provider covers servers without sensitive data. Recovery is handled by the provider. With an institutional provider, the institution's helpdesk handles lost factors. The provider is a single point of trust (T3). A compromised or misconfigured provider can issue tokens that claim 2FA was used. One login prompt. Users whose institution already requires 2FA are not asked again. We can't see the quality of the 2FA. The token says 2FA was used, not whether it was a passkey or SMS, or how the factor can be recovered. Works with our existing OIDC code. Changing providers needs a migration. Account linking makes this manageable.

docs.title: Option B: our own second factor (local broker)
docs.text:
How it works

  • Next to AmCAT or AnnoTinder, the server runs a small OIDC provider of its own (a local broker), e.g. at domain.com/oidc.
  • The broker uses an upstream OIDC provider (e.g. Auth0, Google, an institutional provider) only to verify the user's email address: the first factor.
  • The broker enforces its own second factor (passkeys, TOTP) that can't be reset by email, and sends the same 2FA signal (amr, auth_time) to the apps.
  • For AmCAT and AnnoTinder the broker is just another OIDC provider: they use it as their OIDC_HOST.
Pros Cons Works with any upstream provider that verifies email, including free ones. An extra component that every deployment runs, and that we either adopt or build and maintain. The second factor is independent of the upstream provider (T1, T3). A compromised upstream provider or hijacked inbox is not enough for sensitive actions. Every deployment handles recovery. Each server needs an admin who can verify users and reset factors. We know the quality of the 2FA (e.g. phishing-resistant passkeys, T4). Two login prompts for users whose institution already requires 2FA. Changing the upstream provider is invisible to the apps. They only see the broker's iss and sub; the broker links the new upstream login to the existing identity. Less familiar. It deviates from the common pattern, so it needs explaining to auditors and colleagues.

docs.title: Existing tools
docs.text: Some OIDC providers can act as such a broker, for instance Rauthy (upstream login providers, passkeys and TOTP, lightweight). At the time of writing Rauthy is pre-1.0, and its upstream provider support is described as beta.

docs.title: Precedents
docs.text:
Option A is the common pattern, but option B also has precedents:

  • NIST SP 800-63C-4 (US federal guidelines for federated login). At its highest assurance level (FAL3), the relying party must verify that the user controls an authenticator in addition to the provider's assertion. This can be a bound authenticator that the relying party manages itself, and the provider never sees. NIST presents this as extra protection against a compromised provider (T3).
  • GitLab (self-hosted). Users can sign in via external providers, and GitLab can enforce its own 2FA on top. Administrators can choose to skip GitLab's 2FA for specific providers they trust.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: A: provider handles 2FA B: local broker Follows the common pattern Yes No Security-critical code we maintain None The broker (adopted or built) Provider requirements 2FA and a usable 2FA signal Verified email only Cheapest setup with real 2FA Our shared provider, or a free plan with 2FA (e.g. ZITADEL Cloud) Any free provider plus the broker Stolen password or inbox (T1) Protected Protected Compromised or misconfigured provider (T3) Not protected Protected for sensitive actions Phishing (T4) Depends on the provider's factors Protected with passkeys Account recovery (T5) The provider (e.g. institution helpdesk) Each deployment's admin Changing providers Migration (account linking or re-claiming) Invisible to the apps Prompts for users with institutional 2FA One Two

docs.title: Why B can be added later
docs.text:
Option B doesn't require changes to AmCAT or AnnoTinder. Both apps only talk OIDC to whatever OIDC_HOST points to, and check the same 2FA claim. A local broker is just another OIDC provider. So:

  • We can build A now, and add B later as an extra deployment option.
  • A and B can be used side by side: a deployment with a good institutional provider uses it directly (A), a deployment with a simple provider puts the broker in front of it (B).
  • Account linking and the identities table, which we need for A anyway, also cover moving a deployment from A to B.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
Start with option A, and consider option B later.

  • A is the standard approach, and keeps 2FA, account recovery and phishing-resistance with providers that are managed by security teams.
  • A requires the least security-critical code in our products.
  • A's main weakness, that teams without a suitable provider would have no 2FA, is covered by our shared provider for servers without sensitive data.
  • B solves problems that A can't (provider compromise, providers without 2FA), but adds a component to maintain. Because B can be added without changing the apps, we don't need to decide on it now.

We should reconsider B when:

  • teams report that they can't get a suitable provider with 2FA,
  • a lightweight OIDC provider that supports upstream login with its own enforced 2FA reaches a stable release (e.g. Rauthy 1.0), or
  • passkeys become the default login at the providers our users rely on.

docs.title: Authentication provider
docs.text:
Our software doesn't handle passwords or second factors itself: it delegates logins to an OIDC provider (see the Authentication standard). This page is for teams that host AmCAT or AnnoTinder themselves, and need to choose that provider.

What the lab uses: its own Keycloak, for the lab's own servers (Keycloak VM). It is not a service for other teams' servers, but its setup and realm files (deploy-keycloak) can serve as an example if you decide to run your own Keycloak.

What the provider must do (requirements): verify email addresses, support 2FA and signal it to the server, and support step-up (max_age and auth_time). Which provider fits depends on your institution and on the data on your server:

  1. Your institution's identity provider, or another provider that meets the requirements. Required for sensitive research data.
  2. For teaching and other servers without sensitive data: a provider that doesn't meet all requirements, with weaker security settings.

Your team is responsible for the personal data on your server, and needs its own privacy statement; the lab's privacy statement can serve as an example. Moving to another provider later is a migration.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery: for most universities, the institution's own identity provider. Talk to your IT department: they decide which providers may be used for research data, and may already have one available.

Provider 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM) Notes Your institution's identity provider Depends on the provider Recommended for research data. Ask your IT department. SURFconext (Dutch institutions) acr:<SURFsecureID LoA> 2FA via SURFsecureID, which institutions procure separately. Arranged by your institution. SURF SRAM (Dutch institutions) TODO: verify For research collaborations, including members from other institutions (eduGAIN) and guests (eduID). Every user logs in with 2FA. Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace amr:mfa Institutional accounts. Entra ID needs amr as an optional claim; Google only includes amr when the information is available, so test it. ZITADEL Cloud amr:mfa (verify) Free plan for small teams (100 daily active users), EU data region. You handle account recovery yourself. Use one instance per team. Self-hosted Keycloak amr:mfa Like the lab's own. Only as secure as its maintenance: someone has to keep it updated and handle account recovery.

Not suitable where 2FA is required: the Auth0 free plan (no step-up) and Google consumer accounts (@gmail.com, no institutional agreements, and amr is not always present). The 2FA signals were checked in November 2026 (details and sources); provider behaviour changes, so test the setup before going live. The full evaluation, including Authentik and Auth0: Provider comparison.

docs.title: Teaching and low-sensitivity servers
docs.text:
For a server without sensitive data, such as a course or a pilot, a provider that doesn't meet all requirements can be used, with one or both of the weaker security settings:

  • AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true when the provider has no 2FA, or can't signal it. Sensitive actions (API keys, changing roles) then only need a recent login. Everyone understands the limitation: whoever has a user's password can act as that user.
  • AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true only when the provider does verify email addresses but doesn't send email_verified. Never with a provider where users can choose an address without proving they own it: roles given to an email address could then be claimed by someone else.

Both settings show a permanent warning on the admin page. If the server later gets sensitive data, choose a provider that meets the requirements and migrate first.

docs.title: Checklist for your own provider
docs.text:
• The provider is approved by your institution for the data on your server.
  • The provider returns email_verified: true for your users.
  • 2FA is required (or can be requested) for your users, and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM matches the provider's signal. (Or, for a teaching server only: AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true.)
  • Step-up works: performing a sensitive action (e.g. creating an API key) after more than AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE seconds asks for 2FA again.
  • It is clear who handles account recovery for your users (a helpdesk, or your own admin).
  • The server admin page shows no hardening warnings, or only the ones you chose deliberately.
  • If you are moving from another provider: follow the Migration guide.

docs.title: Migration guide: changing OIDC providers
docs.text: This guide is for teams that move their AmCAT or AnnoTinder server to a different OIDC provider, for instance from a hosted provider used for a pilot to their institution's provider. The person hosting the server is responsible for the migration.

docs.title: Why migration needs care
docs.text:
The OIDC provider is the source of truth for the identity of a user. Our software identifies users by the combination of iss (the provider) and sub (the user at that provider), not by email address (see IBAC). A new provider means a new iss and new sub values, so without a migration the server will not recognize existing users, and all their roles are lost.

There are two strategies:

Account linking JIT re-claiming How users keep their account They link their new login while still logged in with the old one They log in with the new provider and re-claim their account via their email address Relies on email No Yes Both providers needed Yes, during a transition period No Effort for users One extra login during the transition period None Best for Servers with important data, as long as the old provider is still available Servers without sensitive data, or when the old provider is no longer available

docs.title: Account linking
docs.text:
Account linking is the industry standard way to migrate. A user can have multiple login identities (see the identities table in IBAC), so a user can add their new login to their existing account. Because the user is authenticated at both providers when linking, email plays no role.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Move the current provider settings to the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables, set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables, and choose an end date in OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL (e.g. three months ahead). See Configuration.
  3. Users can now log in with either provider. Users who log in with the old provider are asked to link their new login: they sign in at the new provider, and the server adds the new identity to their account.
  4. Remind users before the end date. Server admins can see which users have not linked yet.
  5. After OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL, the old provider is no longer accepted. Remove the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables. Users who did not link can still re-claim their account (see below).

docs.title: JIT re-claiming
docs.text:
With JIT re-claiming, the server forgets the old identities, and users re-claim their account based on their verified email address, using the same JIT account claiming mechanism we use for invitations.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables.
  3. TODO: admin command that removes all identities, turning existing users into shadow users that can be claimed by email.
  4. Users log in with the new provider. If their verified email address matches an existing user, they claim that account.

Risks

Re-claiming relies on email ownership. Someone who controls a user's email address at the new provider (for instance after an address was reassigned) can claim that user's account and roles. Our safeguards limit this: email verification is required (don't use JIT re-claiming with AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION), roles of dormant users are disabled, and unclaimed accounts expire after 3 months. But the risk is not eliminated, so prefer account linking for servers with important data.

For a server without sensitive data (e.g. a teaching server) this is usually acceptable. It is also the fallback for users who missed the account linking transition period.

docs.title: OIDC provider comparison
docs.text:
Evaluation

This page is the evaluation behind our choice of Keycloak (November 2026): the comparison, the hands-on test checklist, and what we found. The decision and its reasons are on the Decisions page. Some use cases below were dropped later: a shared provider for other teams' servers (use case 3, now the lab's own idp), and client registration by others (use cases 2 and 6).

It is only about the provider that the lab runs itself: our software works with any provider that meets the provider requirements.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: # Use case Description 1 Lab authentication Login for the lab's own infrastructure: our AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers, and the AuthWall in front of services without their own login (Whisper, Ollama). Ideally from the same user pool as use case 3, but isolated if that is more secure. 2 Easy client registration Users who host our software can register their server themselves, and get a client ID, client secret and redirect URI configuration. 3 Identity provider One shared pool of users, with one account for all servers that use our provider. We control everything: users can't manage other users or add login methods. 4 Isolated OIDC providers Power users (e.g. a research group) get their own pool of users, and fully manage it themselves: users, login methods, 2FA settings and account recovery. 5 Migration Teams can move to another OIDC provider later (see the Migration guide). 6 Self-registration Users (not power users) can create an account themselves. Client registration starts with limits (e.g. a maximum number of clients) that we can increase. 7 Consent and SSO Single sign-on across all servers, but users consent once per host before a server receives their data. AmCAT and AnnoTinder on the same host count as one host, so one consent covers both.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
These follow from the use cases and the Authentication standard.

  • Consent screen. When other people register clients, the provider must ask users before sharing their data with a client they haven't used before. Without consent, any registered client receives the name and email address of a signed-in user, without the user being asked. That is acceptable only when we register every client ourselves.
  • Tenant isolation. For use cases 1 and 4, users in one pool must not be able to sign in to (or be signed in to) clients of another pool, and this must be enforced by the provider, not by the configuration of each client.
  • Self-service client registration with limits, ideally via the standard (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration, DCR), so that our registration page or tooling stays small.
  • The provider requirements of our standard: email_verified, a 2FA signal (amr or acr), and step-up (max_age, auth_time). Ideally also the option to request 2FA (acr_values), so that users without a second factor are asked to set one up.
  • Little maintenance, and an active project with a clear future.

docs.text: Use case Keycloak Authentik ZITADEL 1. Lab authentication ✅ A separate realm on the same server: its own users, sessions, keys and admins. The AuthWall needs oauth2-proxy. ✅ Built-in forward auth (proxy provider) for the AuthWall. Isolation from the shared pool requires a second installation. ⚠️ Fine for clients we register ourselves. Isolation from the shared pool requires a second installation (see Tenant isolation). 2. Initial access tokens allow a fixed number of registrations, with an expiry date. Or via the admin API. ⚠️ DCR exists in the current source code, with an option to force an authorization flow (e.g. with consent) for registered clients. To verify: max_age. Deployment One container plus PostgreSQL, behind our reverse proxy. Large admin console with many options. Server and worker containers plus PostgreSQL. API and login containers plus PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Teams and future support
docs.text: Keycloak Authentik ZITADEL Who develops it Started at Red Hat (now part of IBM). A CNCF incubating project since April 2023. Red Hat sells a commercial version (Red Hat build of Keycloak). Authentik Security Inc., a small open core company (around 5 to 10 people), backed by Open Core Ventures. MIT license, with paid Enterprise features. ZITADEL, a company in Switzerland that also sells a cloud service. Releases Quarterly feature releases, patch releases every few weeks. Security issues are handled by Red Hat's product security team. Frequent releases. Several critical authentication bypasses in 2026, mostly in features we would not use (SAML sources, proxy, device trust). Frequent releases. Our estimate of future support Very high. Commercially backed, with CNCF governance as a safety net. Medium. Depends on a small company. The MIT license and a large community make a fork possible. Medium to high. Company-backed, with a commercial cloud service.

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text:
The most complete fit for our use cases, and the most battle-tested. Its main cost is complexity: Keycloak has many settings, and a misconfiguration is a bigger risk than the code itself. We manage that by keeping the realm configuration in files in this repository, which Keycloak imports itself (see step 7 of the installation guide), so that it is reviewable and reproducible.

  • Realms give us strong isolation on one server: a realm for the shared pool, a realm for the lab, and a realm per power user.
  • Consent is stored per client. The consent screen is skipped only when the user already approved everything the client asks for.
  • Client registration policies can force consent for every self-registered client, so a registered client can't skip it.
  • Step-up: levels of authentication (acr) can require 2FA on request. Our servers must still check the returned acr themselves, because providers don't always enforce what was requested (see CVE-2026-97176 in Provider support).
  • Deployment: one container and PostgreSQL. start-dev is for local testing only; production needs start with a database, hostname and reverse proxy settings (see the production, reverse proxy and hostname guides).

docs.title: Authentik
docs.text:
Our current lab provider. Simpler than Keycloak, with good forward auth and a built-in consent flow. It covers the identity provider case, but not isolated pools for power users, and it can't request 2FA on demand. It also depends on a small team.

  • Consent: a built-in explicit consent flow, configurable per application.
  • Isolation: one installation is one pool. Multi-tenancy existed for a while, but has been removed.
  • DCR: present in the current source code, including an option to force the authorization flow (e.g. explicit consent) for dynamically registered clients. Its availability in releases and editions needs to be verified.

docs.title: ZITADEL
docs.text:
ZITADEL works well when we register every client ourselves, and the users are ours. It is not suitable for the two other roles we need:

  • Identity provider (use case 3). ZITADEL has no consent screen. A user who is signed in is passed to any registered client without being asked, and the client receives their name and email address. When other people can register clients, users have no say in which clients receive their data. So ZITADEL can't be our identity provider for servers that others run, unless we vet every client.
  • Tenant isolation (use cases 1 and 4). ZITADEL organizations separate user management, but they don't isolate users: whether a client accepts users from other organizations depends on the configuration of that client's project, which is managed by the project's owner. The instance admin can't enforce isolation for all organizations. So separate pools for power users, or for the lab, would each need a separate ZITADEL instance.

docs.title: One client per host
docs.text:
AmCAT and AnnoTinder hosted together on the same host can use the same client ID and client secret. This gives users one consent per host, which matches who actually receives their data: the operator of the host, not the software.

  • Register the redirect URIs and post-logout redirect URIs of both applications on the client.
  • Each application still has its own session (its own session cookie), and logging out is still per application.
  • Both applications share the client secret. Rotating the secret means updating both.
  • Tokens have the same audience for both applications. This is not a problem, because our applications use their own session cookies and don't accept each other's tokens.
  • A client has one back-channel logout URL. Our applications don't use back-channel logout; if that changes, each application needs its own client again.

The Authentication standard describes this as an option.

docs.title: Keycloak test checklist
docs.text:
To be done on a test machine, before migrating anything. Mark items as done, and add findings below each section.

Basics

  • Run Keycloak locally with start-dev, create a realm and a confidential client (authorization code flow with PKCE).
  • Log in to a test application, and check the ID token: email_verified, auth_time, amr.

Consent (use cases 3 and 7)

  • A new user logging in to a client with consent required sees a consent screen.
  • The consent is remembered: a second login to the same client shows no consent screen.
  • AmCAT and AnnoTinder sharing one client on host A: one consent covers both.
  • A client on host B asks for consent again.
  • A silent login (prompt=none) for a user who did not consent returns an error (interaction_required), not a token.
  • Users can see and revoke their consents in the account console (Applications → Remove access); the next login asks for consent again.

Client registration (use cases 2 and 6)

  • Register a client via DCR with an initial access token that allows 2 registrations. A third registration is refused.
  • A client registration policy forces consent for every dynamically registered client.
  • A registered client can't turn off consent afterwards (via the client update endpoint).
  • Trusted hosts or redirect URI restrictions work as expected.
  • To verify: whether a policy exists that keeps new clients disabled until an admin enables them.

Instead of DCR, apps were first registered through our own app registration site, which used the admin API with narrow rights. Since idp is only for the lab's own servers, our admins create the clients, and a client policy turns on consent and PKCE and refuses unsafe redirect URIs (tested, see step 8 of the installation guide). The DCR items above are therefore no longer needed.

Users and 2FA

  • Self-registration with required email verification.
  • amr for password, password plus TOTP, password plus passkey or security key, and a passkey alone: pwd, and pwd + mfa (see the findings for the passkey alone).
  • Step-up: max_age triggers a new login, and auth_time is updated (tested with max_age=5).
  • Requesting 2FA with acr_values: a user without a second factor is asked to set one up. Our server checks the returned acr. (Not used: our setup signals 2FA in amr, and our software does step-up with max_age.)
  • Users can't add login methods (e.g. link other accounts) unless we allow it.

Sessions

  • SSO session lifetime of 30 minutes (idle and maximum).
  • Behaviour on a shared computer after the session ends.

Isolation (use cases 1 and 4)

  • A second realm with a delegated realm admin. That admin can't see or change anything in other realms (tested, see step 4 of the installation guide).
  • A user signed in to one realm is not signed in to another realm.

Migration (use case 5)

  • Export a test realm with users, import it into a fresh Keycloak. Logins work, and user IDs are unchanged.

Operations

  • Production setup with start, PostgreSQL and our reverse proxy (hostname and proxy headers): see the Keycloak installation guide.
  • Realms set up from files with Keycloak's own import (see step 7 of the installation guide).
  • Upgrade from one 26.x release to the next.
  • Backups of the database, and a restore test.
  • oauth2-proxy in front of a service without its own login (the AuthWall).

Findings

Tested with Keycloak 26.8 (locally, with the realm configuration of the installation guide):

  • 2FA flows: mandatory 2FA (with OTP setup for users without a second factor) and optional 2FA both work with Keycloak's built-in conditions, also after Google or GitHub (post login flows). A post login flow in which nothing runs counts as failed: the optional flow needs an "Allow access" step.
  • Copying a flow in the admin console keeps the old flow name in "Condition - sub-flow executed". The copy then silently skips (or repeats) the 2FA step. Hence check-realms.py.
  • amr needs a reference value (pwd, mfa) on each authenticator. Right after setting up OTP during a login, amr contains only pwd (the OTP was set up, not used). After Google or GitHub, amr has no pwd.
  • Account linking in a realm without self-registration: a Google or GitHub login for an unknown email is refused; for an existing account, the user confirms by email first.
  • The admin API refuses tokens of a service account without the default client scope kc-admin-api (401), and checks the roles in the token: with fullScopeAllowed off, a service account loses its admin roles.
  • Delegating clients to their owners works with fine-grained admin permissions (v2): a user sees and edits only their own client in the admin console. But managing those permissions requires manage-realm, which is too much for an automated registration site.
  • Client policies can enforce consent, PKCE and redirect URI rules for changes made by a specific role. The redirect URI rule can only allow http://localhost by allowing http:// in general (our site checks the rest). An empty post logout redirect URI attribute is refused.
  • Client updates keep attributes that are left out; clearing one needs an empty value. Searching clients by attribute is disabled by default.
  • Emails: Keycloak sends the verification email on the first visit to the "verify your email" page (not on the registration form itself), and the password reset email when "forgot password" is submitted. Both only when client_id in the URL is the app of the login, which makes a limit per app in the proxy possible. Resending a verification email right away sends nothing (Keycloak throttles it). With email verification on, Keycloak 26.8 lets new users choose their password only after verifying their email.
  • Email address as username, and changing it: the required action Update email is off by default; without it, users edit their address directly and it is only verified afterwards. With it, the address (and the username) changes only after the new address is confirmed, and the user keeps the same sub, also when they log in with an external provider. The account console only shows the Update email button when Edit username is allowed; the email field stays read-only, and a direct change through the account API is ignored. Changing to an address of another account is refused ("Username already exists"). In a realm without an email server, Update email together with email as username makes accounts without an email address (the bootstrap admin) unable to log in with the admin CLI ("Account is not fully set up").
  • Passkeys: a passkey or security key works as a second factor after the password (amr: pwd + mfa). With "Enable passkeys" (webAuthnPolicyPasswordlessPasskeysEnabled), users can also sign in with only a passkey, but that happens in the step with the password form, so out of the box amr is only pwd, and a flow with mandatory 2FA still asks for OTP. Our flows add a condition ("a passkey was used") that skips the OTP steps and records mfa (tested in all three realms). The account console then offers a passkey twice: under two-factor authentication and under passwordless sign-in.
  • Re-login (max_age) shows the username as text and asks only for the password.
  • Forgot password: Keycloak's default reset credentials flow ends with "Reset OTP", which asks the user to set up a new authenticator app (the old one is kept, with the option "Remove none"), and logs the user in right after the new password, without the second factor (force-login only applies to users from external user stores). So an inbox is enough to get in, and to add an authenticator app. Our flow drops "Reset OTP", and asks users with a second factor for it right after the email link, before the new password; in lab, users without one set up OTP in the same go. Then the user is logged in (tested in lab and idp). (A first version turned force-login on, which makes the user log in again after the new password; that worked but was clumsy for new members.)
  • Required actions run in priority order, not in the order the flow asks for them: by default "Configure OTP" (54) comes before "Update password" (57), so a new member set up the authenticator app before choosing a password. We changed the priorities.
  • Recommending 2FA without forcing it: a required action in a login flow can't be skipped. An app can send the user to the setup with kc_action=CONFIGURE_TOTP: that page has a Cancel button, and the app gets kc_action_status=cancelled or success back (tested). That is the place for a "set up 2FA" recommendation, e.g. on a landing page.
  • Themes can change the texts, CSS and images of the login pages, the account console and emails without changing page templates: a theme with only theme.properties (parent=keycloak.v2) and messages_en.properties. The login header is the message loginTitleHtml, rendered as (sanitized) HTML, so a logo and subtitle need no template; footer.ftl is Keycloak's own place for a custom footer. The account console takes logo, favIcon and styles in theme.properties. Realm overrides (localizationTexts) apply to all theme types, so a changed label (e.g. "Email") also turned up outside the login pages; in a login theme, it stays on the login pages.
  • Partial import of users gives them no roles (not even the realm's default roles), and needs username even with email as username. Without default-roles-<realm>, the account console fails with 401 ("Sorry, an unexpected error has occurred").
  • Recovery codes: the required action Configure OTP has an option Add recovery codes: after setting up an authenticator app (at the first login, or later in the account console), the user sets up recovery codes too. There is no such option after adding a passkey. A recovery code works as a second factor (Try another way), each once (tested).
  • Login action timeout applies to each page of the login, not to the login as a whole: with 20 seconds, 25 seconds on one page restarted the login, while 15 seconds on each of two pages worked (tested).
  • Linking Google or GitHub to an existing account (idp): Keycloak shows "Account already exists", and the user confirms by a link sent to the address, or by the account's password and second factor ("Try another way"). In the latter case, the second factor is asked twice, only this first time: once to confirm the link, and once by the post login flow (tested). After linking, the second factor is asked once.
  • Secrets and realm admins: the file vault keeps secrets out of the database, backups and the admin console (the console shows the reference, e.g. ${vault.smtpPassword}). But a realm admin can reuse the reference: after pointing the realm's SMTP host to another server, Keycloak sent the SMTP password there; a new login provider with ${vault.googleClientSecret} as its secret sent the Google client secret to its token URL. Secrets stored in the database are better protected: the console masks them, and changing a provider's token URL without entering the secret again is refused ("Client secret must be re-entered ..."). Keycloak's SMTP password has no such protection, so email goes through a relay that holds the provider's password, and Keycloak has none to give away (all tested).
  • Realm import: Keycloak's own import (--import-realm) only creates realms that don't exist yet, and only fills in its defaults for parts that are missing from the file entirely: a file with only our own flows gets none of the built-in flows, and a file with one client scope gets none of the default scopes. So the realm files are complete exports (a default realm plus our changes). master is imported too on a new installation, before the temporary admin is created, whose password must then meet the imported password policy. Placeholders for missing environment variables are imported as text. (We first used keycloak-config-cli, a third-party tool that applies changes to existing realms; it needs an admin client with a secret on the server.)

docs.title: Authentication standard
docs.text:
How authentication works in all software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab (AmCAT, AnnoTinder): what the software does, and what it requires from the OIDC provider. It is written for developers of our software. Teams that host the software only need parts of it; these pages link to those:

  • Authentication provider: for teams that host our software.
  • Migration guide: moving to a different OIDC provider.
  • Decisions: why it is set up this way, and which alternatives we dropped.

docs.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
docs.text:
OIDC is an open standard for authentication that builds on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol. It allows clients to verify the identity of users based on the authentication performed by an external identity provider (IdP). By using OIDC, our software does not handle user authentication directly, but delegates it to an external OIDC provider. This is an industry standard, because it outsources the hard part of authentication to a dedicated provider, which is often better equipped to handle it than the application itself.

Our software works with any OIDC provider that meets the provider requirements. The person hosting our software chooses the provider, and is responsible for making sure it is suitable. The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery. Talk to your institution's IT support circle.

docs.title: Choosing an OIDC provider
docs.text:
The person hosting our software chooses the OIDC provider (see Authentication provider):

  • Your institution's identity provider (recommended, and the right choice for sensitive research data): managed by a security team, with a helpdesk for account recovery.
  • Another provider that meets the requirements, hosted (e.g. ZITADEL Cloud) or self-hosted (e.g. Keycloak). The lab runs its own Keycloak for its own servers; its documentation (Keycloak VM) can serve as an example.
  • For teaching and other servers without sensitive data: a provider that doesn't meet all requirements, with the weaker security settings turned on.

Names and email addresses of users (e.g. students) are personal data, so any server must be used according to your institution's rules. Moving to another provider is a migration. For development on a local machine there is a separate development mode.

docs.title: OIDC provider requirements
docs.text:
By default, the provider must meet all three requirements. The first two can be turned off, for teaching and other servers without sensitive data (see Weaker security).

Requirement What the provider must do Email verification Return "email_verified": true in the ID token. Our software uses email addresses to assign roles (see Authorization). 2FA with a usable signal Support 2FA, and signal in the ID token that it was used. Providers do this differently (amr containing mfa, or a specific acr value), so the claim is configured with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. See Provider support for MFA signals. Step-up Honour the max_age parameter (re-authenticate if the last login is older than N seconds), and return auth_time in the ID token. This one can't be turned off.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Proposed names; to be aligned with the AmCAT and AnnoTinder code.

Variable Required Description OIDC_HOST yes Issuer URL of the trusted OIDC provider. OIDC_CLIENT_ID yes Client ID registered at the provider. OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET yes Client secret registered at the provider. OIDC_MFA_CLAIM no Which claim counts as 2FA: amr:mfa (default) or acr:<value>, e.g. acr:http://test.surfconext.nl/assurance/loa2 for SURFconext. AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE no Maximum age in seconds of the last 2FA login for sensitive actions. Default: 600. OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_PREVIOUS_MFA_CLAIM no The previous OIDC provider, only during a migration. OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL no Date after which the previous provider is no longer accepted. AUTH_DEV_MODE no Enables development mode. Refused unless the server only listens on localhost. AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA no true turns off the 2FA requirement (see Weaker security). AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION no true turns off the email verification requirement (see Weaker security).

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
For sensitive actions (e.g. creating API keys, changing roles) our servers require a 2FA login that is at most AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE seconds old (step-up authentication).

  1. The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time in the ID token.
  2. If the claim is missing or too old, the server redirects the user to the OIDC provider with max_age.
  3. The server checks the new ID token itself, because providers do not always enforce what was requested.

With AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA, steps 1 to 3 only check auth_time: sensitive actions still need a recent login, but not a second factor.

Account recovery (e.g. a lost phone) is the responsibility of the OIDC provider.

docs.title: Weaker security: teaching and low-sensitivity servers
docs.text:
Two requirements can be turned off, each with its own setting. Both are deliberately named INSECURE: they make the server less secure, and must never be used for servers with sensitive research data. In .env:

# Weaker security: only for teaching and other servers without sensitive data.
# See https://vu-societal-analytics.github.io/societal-analytics-lab-infra/auth/#weaker-security-teaching-and-low-sensitivity-servers
AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true
AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true

  • Sensitive actions (e.g. creating API keys, changing roles) no longer require a second factor, but still require a recent login (step-up with max_age and auth_time).
  • The server still records whether a login used 2FA (has_mfa, with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM), so admins can see who uses it anyway.
  • Risk: anyone who gets hold of a user's password, or their email (to reset it), can perform that user's sensitive actions.

AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

  • Users can log in when the provider doesn't confirm their email address (email_verified is false or missing). The server records what the provider sent (email_verified in the user table).
  • Roles given to an email address (invitations, see JIT account claiming) can still be claimed by a user whose address is not verified. That is the risk: on a provider where people can choose their own address, someone could claim the roles meant for someone else. Only use this setting with a provider that does verify addresses but doesn't send the claim (e.g. some institutional providers).
  • Roles based on the email domain, or on having a verified address (ABAC, require_email), still only apply to users with email_verified = true.

Both settings:

  • The server logs a warning at every start.
  • The admin page permanently shows them as hardening warnings.
  • Turning a setting off again restores the requirement: users who don't meet it can no longer log in (email) or perform sensitive actions (2FA).

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Our software also supports direct API access via API keys. These are application-managed tokens that are decoupled from the OIDC provider.

  • API keys can only be created and changed by the main web client, in a session that passed step-up authentication.
  • API keys always have a limited scope.

docs.title: Server hardening warnings
docs.text:
The web client shows server admins a list of warnings for things that make the server less secure:

Warning Meaning 2FA not required AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA is set: sensitive actions don't need a second factor. Not for sensitive data (see Weaker security). Email verification not required AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION is set. Not for sensitive data. Roles for unverified email addresses Users with roles whose provider did not confirm their email address (email_verified = false). Check that these are the right people. No 2FA signal Recent logins did not contain the configured OIDC_MFA_CLAIM, so sensitive actions are blocked. Check the provider's 2FA settings and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. (Not shown with AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA.) Migration not finished OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST is still configured after OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL.

docs.title: Development mode
docs.text: AUTH_DEV_MODE lets developers run our software on their own machine without an OIDC provider, logged in as a local admin. The server refuses to start in development mode unless it only listens on localhost. Development mode is never used for servers that other people use.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
All software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab follows these rules, to ensure consistency and security across our software stack.

Rule Details Same origin The server and web client are always hosted on the same domain. Server-side OIDC flow The server initiates and completes the OIDC flow with the trusted provider (OIDC_HOST), and sets a signed, http-only session cookie. Scopes The server requests the scopes openid email, nothing more. It uses sub, email, email_verified, the 2FA signal and auth_time, and no name, so users aren't asked to share more than needed. One session per application When AmCAT and AnnoTinder are hosted together, each application has its own session. They can share one OIDC client (the same client ID and client secret), so that users consent once per host (see One client per host). The second login completes without user interaction, because the user is already signed in at the provider. Logging out is per application. Authorization on the server The server decides what users may do, not the OIDC provider (see Authorization). API keys for other clients Other clients (e.g. R or Python) can only access the backend via API keys. Email verification The server checks the email_verified claim, unless AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION is set (see Weaker security). 2FA and step-up The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time for sensitive actions, and performs step-up authentication if needed (see Two-factor authentication). AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA drops the OIDC_MFA_CLAIM check, not the step-up.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Authorization is based on roles. A role can be given to a specific user (IBAC), to users with a certain attribute (ABAC), or both.

docs.title: Role table
docs.text: Column Description role What role a user has (e.g. READ, WRITE, ADMIN). context The context in which the role applies (e.g. project, server). user_id If not null, the role is linked to a specific user (see IBAC). email_domain If not null, the user's verified email (email_verified = true) must have this domain (see ABAC). Can be combined with user_id to require both. require_email If user_id and email_domain are null: whether any user gets the role (false), or only users with a verified email address (true). granted_at When the role was granted (created, updated, or restored).

docs.title: Identity Based Access Control (IBAC)
docs.text:
IBAC is the primary mode of authorization: roles are given to registered users.

The identity is iss + sub, not the email address. An email address is not a unique identifier, because it can change over time: users can change email addresses, and old email addresses can be reassigned. We do use the email address as a human readable way to assign roles (e.g. giving a colleague access to a project in AmCAT). This is safe, because the role is not assigned to the email address itself, but to the user (iss + sub) that currently owns it. Changing email addresses is the responsibility of the OIDC provider: when the email for an identity has changed, the server updates the user table.

Any user that signs in is registered, optionally with a form that collects additional information. We use this for security logs and rate limiting, which is legitimate under GDPR. Email addresses add some accountability, especially when roles require an email domain.

User table

Column Description id Unique user ID. email Email address of the user, from the most recent login. email_verified Whether the provider confirmed the email address at the most recent login: true only if it sent email_verified: true, otherwise false. NULL for shadow users. Without AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION, only users with true can log in. has_mfa Whether the most recent login contained the 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM). Shown on the admin page, without a warning: 2FA is only needed for sensitive actions. registered_at When the user first signed in. NULL for shadow users until the account is claimed (see JIT account claiming). last_login_at When the user last signed in. reactivated_at First login after 1 year of inactivity. ... Optional user details (e.g. added on registration).

Identities table

Column Description user_id The user this identity belongs to. iss Issuer of the OIDC provider. sub Unique subject identifier at the OIDC provider. linked_at When the identity was linked to the user. last_login_at When the user last signed in with this identity.

Normally a user has one identity. A user can have more than one during a migration to a new OIDC provider.

docs.title: JIT account claiming
docs.text: Just-In-Time (JIT) account claiming lets us give roles to an email address that is not yet registered. The role is given to a new shadow user, which only has an id and email (registered_at is NULL, and there is no identity yet). The current owner of the email address is invited to claim the account and role. This can be an actual invitation, or just happen automatically when they first sign in. Claiming adds an identity and sets registered_at.

docs.title: Safeguards against email reassignment
docs.text:
Two safeguards prevent giving a role to a previous or future owner of an email address. A role is not given to a user if one of these conditions is true:

Dormant users. A role is disabled when:

role.granted_at < user.reactivated_at AND NOT user.has_mfa
  • Why: without 2FA, the OIDC provider only verifies current ownership of the email address. So after a year of inactivity, roles granted before reactivation are disabled. With 2FA required this should be rare, but it remains a safeguard for accounts claimed via email and providers that report 2FA inconsistently.
  • Restore: per role (e.g. an AmCAT project ADMIN refreshes granted_at), or by a server admin.

Expired invitations. A role is not given when:

user.registered_at > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'
  • Why: a role given to an unregistered email address must be claimed within 3 months, so that a future owner of the address can't claim it. Roles granted after registration are not affected, because then granted_at is later than registered_at.
  • Unclaimed invitations: a shadow user that is still unclaimed (registered_at IS NULL) has an expired invitation when now() > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'.
  • Restore: remove the invitation, or restore it by updating granted_at.

docs.title: Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC)
docs.text:
ABAC is the secondary mode of authorization: roles are given based on user attributes from OIDC claims. We currently only use the email domain, because this keeps the role of the OIDC provider restricted to authentication and email verification. In the future we could include other attributes (e.g. eduPerson claims from institutional providers).

IBAC and ABAC serve different purposes:

IBAC ABAC Based on Identities, tied to specific users Attributes, properties of users that can change Use Users keep their roles when they change email addresses. Important for long-term projects where researchers change institutions. Give and take away access based on a user's current situation, such as their affiliation with an institution.

Email domains are useful for:

  • Convenience: give access to anyone with an institutional email address, instead of giving everyone individual access. This should have limited privileges (never ADMIN).
  • Security: restrict access to a trusted institution. Combined with IBAC, access is restricted to a trusted person who also has a verified email address at that institution.

docs.title: Backup strategies
docs.text: Background for the lab's backups: the common approaches, and how our setup relates to them. How it is set up: Backups.

docs.title: What a backup must survive
docs.text: Risk Example What protects against it A mistake A deleted file, a failed upgrade, a bug that corrupts data Backups with history (yesterday, last week, last month), even on the same server Losing the server A broken disk, a deleted VM, a fire A copy somewhere else An attacker or ransomware Someone with access to the server deletes or encrypts everything A copy the server itself can't delete or change A backup that doesn't work The job stopped months ago; the backups can't be read Monitoring, checks, and restore tests

docs.title: Common principles
docs.text:
• 3-2-1: three copies of the data (the original and two backups), on two kinds of storage, one of them elsewhere. A backup on the same server is not a backup against losing that server.
  • History: keep several versions, e.g. 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly ("grandfather-father-son"). A mistake is often noticed late, and a backup that only has last night's version has the mistake too.
  • Encryption: backups contain everything, including personal data and secrets. Encrypting them on the server, before they leave it, means the place where they are stored never sees the data. The key must be stored safely, apart from the backups: without it, the backups are useless.
  • Consistent copies of databases: a database writes to its files all the time, so a file copy of a running database can be inconsistent and fail to load. Databases are backed up with their own tool (a dump: pg_dump for PostgreSQL), or by stopping them, or with a snapshot of the whole disk.
  • Monitoring: a backup job that stops is easy to miss. The usual approach is a "dead man's switch": the job reports every run to a monitoring service, which raises an alarm when a report is missing, so it also notices a job that didn't run at all.
  • Restore tests: a backup is only proven when it has been restored. Test a restore after setting up, and regularly afterwards.
  • Retention, both ways: backups also keep data that was deleted on purpose (e.g. after a retention period). How long backups are kept is part of the privacy statement.

docs.title: Server backups and app backups
docs.text:
Server backups App backups What A copy of the whole server (its disk) Per app: its settings, its files, and its databases as dumps Who Usually the IT department or the platform The people who run the app Good for Losing a whole server: everything back at once Restoring one app, one file, or one database to an earlier state; moving an app to another server Weak point Coarse (all or nothing); a running database in it may be inconsistent; we don't control how long it's kept Only covers what each app set up

Most organizations use both: server backups as the last resort, and app backups for everyday restores.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• restic and borg: the most used open-source tools for file backups. Both encrypt on the server, store only changes (deduplication), keep history with one command, and check their own backups. restic can store backups almost anywhere (local, SFTP, S3 and more); borg works best with SSH.
  • borgmatic and resticprofile: configuration files around borg and restic, including database dumps and monitoring, for larger setups.
  • Database dumps in Docker: a small service in the app's compose file that runs pg_dump on a schedule, writing to a folder that the file backup picks up.
  • Monitoring: healthchecks.io (hosted, or self-hosted) and similar services receive a ping per run.

docs.title: Our setup
docs.text:
• Server backups by VU IT as the last resort. TODO: confirm with VU IT what they cover.
  • App backups: every app keeps what it needs to be restored under /opt/<app>, with a database backup service per database (Docker Compose standards). Every night, restic backs up /opt, encrypted, keeps 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly backups, checks them (on Sundays also a 5% sample of the data), and reports to healthchecks.io.
  • Data with a short retention is in named volumes that our backups don't contain, with a cleanup service that deletes it after the retention period.

Where we stand against the principles above:

Principle Status History Yes: 7 daily, 4 weekly, 6 monthly Encryption Yes: restic, key in the password manager Consistent databases Yes: daily dumps by the apps Monitoring Yes: healthchecks.io, which also notices a missing run A copy elsewhere (3-2-1) Not yet: our backups are on the same server. TODO: a location with VU IT Safe from an attacker on the server Not yet: the server can delete its own backups. A location the server can only add to (e.g. S3 with object lock) would solve this. Restore tests To do after setup, then twice a year

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The choices behind the lab's setup: what was chosen, why, and which alternatives were dropped. The other pages describe how things are; this page explains why. The evaluations behind these decisions: 2FA: where should it live? and Provider comparison.

Last reviewed: November 2026.

docs.title: OIDC for all our software
docs.text:
Chosen: AmCAT and AnnoTinder delegate logins to an OIDC provider, and work with any provider that meets our requirements.

Why: logins, passwords, second factors and account recovery are the provider's job, done by people who specialize in it; our software contains no password or 2FA code. The person hosting a server can use the provider their institution already has.

docs.title: Requirements: verified email, 2FA signal, step-up
docs.text:
Chosen: by default, the provider must confirm email addresses (email_verified), signal 2FA (amr or acr), and support step-up (max_age, auth_time). Our software checks the tokens itself.

Why: roles can be given to an email address, so the address must be verified. Sensitive actions (API keys, roles) need a recent login with a second factor. Providers don't always enforce what is asked of them, so our software checks the result itself instead of trusting the request. See the Authentication standard.

docs.title: 2FA lives at the OIDC provider
docs.text:
Chosen: the second factor is part of the login at the provider (option A in 2FA: where should it live?).

Dropped (for now): a local broker on each server (option B), which would add its own second factor on top of any provider. It would make the second factor independent of the provider, but each server would then run a security-critical login service, with an admin page for recovery that has to be exposed and protected too. Setting that up properly is harder than a clear, visible limitation. Option B needs no change to our software, so it can still be added later (see Later).

docs.title: Weaker security for teaching: two explicit settings
docs.text:
Chosen: AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA and AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION (Weaker security). Both are off by default, named "insecure", logged at every start, and shown permanently on the admin page.

Why: teams need an easy way to run a server for teaching or a pilot, with whatever login they have. A limitation that everyone understands ("this server doesn't require 2FA") is better than a complex setup that is easy to get wrong.

Dropped:

  • A shared OIDC provider run by the lab for other teams' servers (the idp realm with self-service app registration). It would make us responsible for the availability of their servers, and for recovering their users' second factors, and as the operator we could log in as any of their users. See The idp realm.
  • OIDC_MFA_CLAIM=none: reads like a harmless default, not like a deliberate weakening.
  • A setting that "trusts" the provider's email addresses: we record email_verified = false when the claim is missing, so we don't trust it; we skip the check. Hence a flag of the same kind as the 2FA flag.

docs.title: email_verified and has_mfa in the user table
docs.text:
Chosen: the user table records email_verified (what the provider sent at the last login: true, otherwise false; NULL for shadow users) next to has_mfa. The admin page warns about users with roles and an unverified address; has_mfa is shown without a warning, because 2FA is only needed for sensitive actions.

Why: with AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION, admins must be able to see who could claim roles without a verified address. Later, our software could verify addresses itself (see Later).

docs.title: The identity provider of the lab
Keycloak
docs.text:
Chosen: one Keycloak installation for the lab (Keycloak VM).

What the lab needs:

  • Our Authentication standard: verified email (email_verified), a 2FA signal (amr), and step-up (max_age, auth_time).
  • A login for services without their own (the lab login on the lab server), through forward auth.
  • External collaborators: researchers from other institutions, including abroad, and guests without an institutional account.
  • Little maintenance, and a clear route for account recovery: lab admins can reset a member's second factor.

Why Keycloak:

  • Realms: separate logins (users, sessions, keys, admins) in one installation: lab, idp, and later realms for other teams.
  • Everything our standard needs: email_verified, amr (with our configuration), step-up with max_age, and it can also be asked for 2FA (acr_values). Consent per client, enforced by client policies.
  • Realm files: the configuration of a realm is a file in the repository, which documents it and sets it up again.
  • A mature project with a large community, backed by Red Hat and the CNCF.

Dropped:

  • Authentik (our previous provider): no isolated pools within one installation (its multi-tenancy was removed), and it depends on a small company. It also can't be asked for 2FA: an app can't send acr_values to make Authentik require a second factor; whether 2FA is asked depends only on the login flow. With our step-up (max_age, checking amr) that matters little, as long as the flow asks for 2FA from everyone who has it.
  • ZITADEL: no consent screen (any registered app gets the data of a signed-in user), and its organizations don't isolate users.
  • SURF SRAM as our provider: less control (we can't reset 2FA or recover accounts ourselves), depends on approval by the university, and not suitable for our open idp. It may become a login option of lab (see Later).

The comparison and the hands-on tests: Provider comparison.

docs.title: lab and idp are separate realms
docs.text:
Chosen: lab (the lab's infrastructure: members added by us, mandatory 2FA, no Google or GitHub) and idp (the lab's AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers: open sign-up, optional 2FA) are separate realms.

Dropped: one realm, with roles for lab access and mandatory 2FA per client.

  • Mandatory 2FA per client works badly with single sign-on: after a login without 2FA to one server, the session would also open a lab service, unless Keycloak's levels of authentication are used, the mechanism of a recent bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-97176).
  • Open sign-up in the realm of the lab services: one lab service that forgets its role check would be open to anyone with a Google account. Separate realms make this impossible by design.
  • Different rules: login options, texts, recovery and admins differ between the two.

The cost: lab members have two accounts. lab as a login option of idp solves that later (see Later).

docs.title: The idp realm: the lab's own login, not a public service
docs.text:
Chosen: idp is the one login for the lab's own servers. Anyone can create an account (with email, Google or GitHub), but an account gives no access by itself: each server gives roles. Our admins create the clients of our servers in the admin console; a client policy turns on consent and PKCE and refuses unsafe redirect URIs (step 8 of the installation guide).

Why: students and collaborators sign up themselves when a project gives them access, instead of waiting for an admin. The client policy prevents mistakes, not misuse: admins are trusted.

Servers get the email address and the 2FA signal (and the account ID and login time), and the name only if they ask for it (the scope profile), not roles. Our software only uses the email address and the 2FA signal, so it requests openid email; other services (which often request profile) work too. The consent screen says it in words everyone understands: "see your email address; see whether you signed in with two-factor authentication", plus "see your name" for services that ask for it. Keycloak refuses a request for a scope it doesn't offer (e.g. roles), so only these are offered.

Dropped:

  • idp as a public service for other teams' servers, with the app registration site (where others registered their servers) and email limits per app in tiers. See Weaker security for teaching for why; with only our own servers, these are no longer needed.
  • Closed sign-up in idp: every student and collaborator would have to be added by an admin first.
  • Letting app owners manage their client in the admin console (fine-grained admin permissions): creating those permissions requires a role that can change the whole realm. (No longer relevant without outside app owners.)

docs.title: Login in lab: password and mandatory 2FA
docs.text:
Chosen:

  • Members are added by us, without a password and without an email from us. They set their password themselves with First time, or forgot your password? on the login page. After the email link, in one go: a password, their name, an authenticator app, recovery codes, and they're in (Adding lab members).
  • 2FA is mandatory: these accounts give access to our infrastructure, and a mandatory second factor is needed for lab to become a trusted login option of idp later.
  • "Remember me" keeps members logged in for up to 30 days on their own device.

Dropped:

  • Login with a code or link by email, without passwords: Keycloak can't do this without a third-party extension, and we don't install extensions in our login service.
  • Invitation emails sent by us: members sign up when they need a lab service.
  • Passkeys as the default second factor: many people don't understand them. Passkeys are offered in the account console, and a passkey alone counts as two factors.
  • Optional 2FA in lab, with a recommendation: a login flow can't offer a skippable step. A landing page could recommend 2FA (an app can send users to the 2FA setup with a Cancel button), but lab keeps 2FA mandatory.

docs.title: A password reset never replaces the second factor
docs.text:
Chosen: after the email link, users with a second factor enter it before they can choose a new password (How users log in).

Dropped: Keycloak's default reset, which logs the user in after the new password without the second factor, and lets them set up a new authenticator app, so an inbox was enough to take over an account. Also dropped: a first fix that made users log in again after the reset (secure, but clumsy for new members).

docs.title: Recovery codes, and OTP as the default second factor
docs.text:
Chosen: users who set up an authenticator app (OTP) get recovery codes right after. Where 2FA is mandatory, users without a second factor are asked to set up OTP.

Why: OTP works on every device, with any authenticator app. Recovery codes let users recover from a lost phone without us, which matters because email can't be used for that.

docs.title: Our look: texts and CSS only
docs.text:
Chosen: Keycloak themes with the lab logo, colours and our texts, but no changed page templates (Themes).

Why: page templates change between Keycloak versions and can break after an upgrade; texts, CSS and images rarely do. Users see whose login this is.

Dropped: the VU logo (its use is usually restricted to official VU communication; a link to the department page instead), and realm overrides for texts (a changed "Email" label then also showed up outside the login pages).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• One VM, Docker Compose, Keycloak's optimized image: recommended in Running Keycloak in a container; build options are baked in, so starts are faster and predictable.
  • Caddy in front, re-encrypt: the reverse proxy guide prefers re-encrypt over plain HTTP between proxy and Keycloak. Caddy terminates the public TLS connection, so it can filter paths and IP addresses; Keycloak only accepts HTTPS, with an internal, long-lived certificate that only Caddy trusts. (Passthrough would make path and IP filtering impossible.)
  • Only /realms/, /resources/ and /.well-known/ are public: the exposed paths recommended in the reverse proxy guide. The admin consoles, the admin API and the master realm are only on a separate admin hostname, restricted to the university's IP ranges. The ranges are in a local file on the VM, not in the repository; a realm for a team outside the university can get an exception for its own admin console.
  • The health endpoint on plain HTTP (port 9000): only used by the container's health check, and not exposed.
  • All Caddy settings in one mounted folder: Docker keeps showing the old version of a single mounted file after an editor replaces it, so a reload would silently not apply a change.
  • PostgreSQL 18: the version Keycloak 26.8 is tested with.
  • A temporary bootstrap admin, replaced by a permanent admin with 2FA (Bootstrapping and recovering an admin account).

docs.title: Realm files, imported by Keycloak itself
docs.text:
Chosen: complete realm files, imported by Keycloak's own --import-realm when a realm doesn't exist yet (Realms). Later changes are made in the admin console.

Dropped: keycloak-config-cli, a third-party tool that applies the files again and again. It needs an admin client with a secret on the server, for a workflow we don't use.

docs.title: The email relay, and secrets admins can use but not take
docs.text:
Chosen: Keycloak sends all email through a relay on the VM, without a password; only the relay holds the email provider's password. It also caps all email, accepts only our sender address, and queues mail. The Google and GitHub secrets of idp are stored masked in Keycloak, which requires them again when a provider is pointed elsewhere.

Why: a realm admin can change a realm's email server. With Keycloak's own SMTP login, Keycloak would send the password to whatever server they enter. This is an extra layer, not a wall: admins can send email and use the Google and GitHub logins, and a real admin can always replace the secrets, but not read them out. It matters most once other teams get their own realm.

Dropped: Keycloak's file vault for the secrets: a realm admin can use a vault reference anywhere, and so send the secret to their own server (tested).

docs.title: Email limits
docs.text:
Chosen: a limit per IP address in Caddy, on the requests that make Keycloak send an email, and a cap on all email in the relay (Email limits).

Why: Keycloak has no limit on the emails it sends, and its brute force detection only covers logins. Blocking only the requests that send an email never breaks logins or the sessions of a server. The cap on all email is in the relay, because only the relay counts emails that were actually sent; a limit on all requests in Caddy could be used up by one person.

Dropped: limits per app, in tiers (only needed while others could register apps), and disabling a client that sends too much email (it would also break the logins and refresh grants of that server, and could be abused to block it).

docs.title: One system account, every app in /opt with Docker Compose, Caddy on the server, Docker with sudo
docs.text:
Chosen: every app in /opt/<app>, owned by the system account sal (no login, no home directory); admins are in the sal group and work as sal with sudo -u sal and sudoedit -u sal. Caddy runs on the server itself and is the only way in. Admins run Docker with sudo. The same on the service VMs (Apps on our servers).

Why: one convention for all apps on a server with many small apps, and no app files owned by root or by an admin's personal account. Caddy in front of everything gives HTTPS and one place to decide what is reachable.

Every app runs with Docker Compose, from /opt/<app>/compose.yml: one way of working, so the examples on Docker Compose standards apply to every app, and its whole setup can be read in one file. Apps the lab maintains itself (Keycloak, the backup job) have their own repository, cloned to /opt/<app>; apps we only host have a compose.yml written from the examples.

Two layers of backups: VU IT's server backups as the last resort, and our own backups per app (Backup strategies). Everything needed to restore an app is under /opt/<app>: its compose.yml and .env, its files in data/, and its databases as dumps in backups/, made every day by a backup service in its own compose file. Every night, restic backs up /opt, encrypted, keeps 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly backups, checks them, and reports to healthchecks.io, which emails us when a backup failed or didn't run (Backups).

Why:

  • Databases are dumped, because a copy of a running database's files can be inconsistent.
  • The apps dump their own databases, in a container of their own compose file. A script on the server that runs per-app commands as root would let anyone who can change an app's files (sal) run code as root.
  • Data with a short retention is in named volumes, which our backups don't contain, with a cleanup service in the same compose file (or the app's own setting): the retention policy sits next to the app, and deleted data doesn't live on in our backups.
  • Monitoring by a "dead man's switch" (healthchecks.io) also notices a backup that didn't run at all, and needs no mail credentials on the servers.

Dropped:

  • sal in the docker group: membership of that group is effectively root access, and apps that run as sal without Docker would get it too.
  • Backing up all Docker volumes as well: they contain the raw files of running databases (unreliable, and large) and caches. With VU IT's server backups as the last resort, our backups only need what each app sets up.
  • Dump scripts per app run by the backup job as root (hooks.d, or /opt/<app>/backup.sh): see above.
  • A policy file per app read by our own tool: the compose file already declares the app's backup and retention, with standard images.
  • Data in /srv/<app>: two places per app instead of one. A separate data disk would be a reason to revisit this.
  • Retention with systemd-tmpfiles on the server: works, but the rule then lives outside the app's compose file, and needs a step on the server per app.
