  • One repository with everything (documentation and deployments): the apps then lived deep inside a clone (/opt/keycloak/societal-analytics-lab-infra/deploy/keycloak), and every server cloned all of it.

docs.title: All lab services under lab., with one login cookie for the zone
docs.text:
Chosen: every service the lab runs for its members gets an address under lab.societal-analytics.nl (e.g. whisper.lab.societal-analytics.nl), with or without its own login, and lab.societal-analytics.nl is the overview page. Services without their own login sit behind oauth2-proxy with Caddy's forward_auth, against the lab realm. oauth2-proxy sets one login cookie for the zone (.lab.societal-analytics.nl), and every login comes back to one fixed address (lab.societal-analytics.nl/oauth2/callback). Signing out ends the login for all services and the Keycloak session (oauth2-proxy's backend logout). oauth2-proxy checks the session with Keycloak every 10 minutes, so inactive users (2 hours, Keycloak's idle time) and removed members are signed out (Lab server).

Why: users need one login, and one sign-out that ends everything. oauth2-proxy can't do that with a cookie per service: a browser only lets a site clear its own cookies, and oauth2-proxy doesn't support Keycloak's back-channel logout. A shared cookie is the common way to use oauth2-proxy, but a cookie for the whole domain would also go to the lab's website, which is hosted by GitHub Pages. A zone of its own keeps the cookie within the lab's own services on this server, which could reach each other anyway. The zone also makes the rule visible: everything under lab. is a lab service.

The condition: only services the lab runs on its own servers may be under lab.. A site hosted by someone else would receive a login that works for all services behind the lab login (the cookie isn't bound to one service).

oauth2-proxy in a Docker network of its own, with its port published on 127.0.0.1 only, and only the gateway of that network trusted for X-Forwarded-* headers. It can't reach the apps on the server's localhost, and no other container can reach it.

Dropped:

  • A cookie per service: signing out of one service would leave the others logged in until their next check with Keycloak. (oauth2-proxy also doesn't bind a cookie to a service, so it protected less than it seemed.)
  • One cookie for the whole domain: it would be sent to the website on GitHub Pages.
  • Services under one address, by path (lab.societal-analytics.nl/whisper): all services would share one origin, so their cookies could clash, and a bug in one could read the others' pages; many apps also can't run under a sub-path.
  • A wildcard redirect URI (https://*.lab.societal-analytics.nl/...): Keycloak doesn't allow a wildcard in the host name (tested). One fixed callback replaces it.
  • network_mode: host for oauth2-proxy (simpler, but a compromised oauth2-proxy could reach every app on the server's localhost).
  • A CMS for the website on the lab server: the public website stays on GitHub Pages (quick updates, nothing to maintain); the overview page of lab services is a static page behind the lab login.

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
• "Sign in with your lab account" in idp: lab as a login option of idp, so lab members use one account. A login through lab (which always requires 2FA) could count as 2FA in idp, if step-up works: idp must pass a request for a fresh login (max_age) on to lab. To be tested.
  • Institutional login for lab, via SURF SRAM (below).
  • A local broker (option B) as a deployment option, if the field moves towards passkeys that sync across devices, or a lightweight broker with upstream login and enforced 2FA matures (see 2FA: where should it live?).
  • Recommending 2FA in idp on a landing page of the lab's services: an app can send users to the 2FA setup with a Cancel button (kc_action), and learns whether they set it up.
  • Verifying email addresses in our software, for servers with their own email server, so that email_verified can become true without the provider.

docs.title: Institutional login via SRAM
docs.text:
SURF Research Access Management (SRAM) is SURF's service for research collaborations: members log in with their own institution (VU, or other institutions worldwide via eduGAIN), or with eduID if they have no institutional account. The VU already uses SRAM, for instance for Yoda.

Keycloak can offer SRAM as a login option of the lab realm (as an external OIDC provider), so lab members and collaborators could log in with their institution, while the lab's services keep talking to Keycloak, with the same claims. Open questions:

  • Does SRAM's ID token include email_verified, a 2FA signal (amr/acr), and auth_time, and does it honour max_age? If SRAM enforces 2FA but doesn't signal it, the lab realm would still ask for its own second factor.
  • SRAM depends on the VU: the lab may need to request a collaboration, and service registrations are reviewed. Each service needs a privacy policy and an acceptable use policy (privacy statement, AUP).
  • lab fits such a review well: a known list of lab services, for lab members and invited collaborators. idp, open to anyone, would be much harder to justify as a login service that passes identities on.

The next step is a test on SRAM's acceptance environment (acc.sram.surf.nl). Sources: SURF Research Access Management (SURF wiki), VU Research Support Handbook: SRAM invitations and eduID, SRAM setup guide.

docs.title: About this section
docs.text:
The pages in this section record recent decisions and the information behind them: what was chosen, which alternatives were considered, and the evaluations that led there. They are not set in stone: when circumstances change (new requirements, a provider that changes its behaviour, feedback from VU IT), the decisions can be revisited, and these pages are where that discussion starts.

  • Decisions: the choices behind the current setup.
  • 2FA: where should it live?: whether the second factor belongs at the login provider or in our software.
  • Provider comparison: the identity providers that were evaluated and tested.
  • Backup strategies: common approaches to backups, and how ours relate to them.
  • Hardening plan: what else to do to make the infrastructure harder to break into (SSH only from the VU network, security keys, quick updates, access to the VMs through the portal).

docs.title: Hardening plan
docs.text:
What else to do to make the lab's infrastructure harder to break into, beyond what is set up now. The aim is a setup that is safe and simple: every step here is cheap, easy to understand, and hard to get wrong. More elaborate options are at the end, for when there is a concrete reason. Nothing on this page is in place yet, unless it says so.

The most sensitive machine is the Keycloak VM: whoever controls it controls every login of the lab.

docs.title: Where we stand
docs.text:
• SSH to the VMs: keys only, no root logins (University VMs).
  • Keycloak's admin consoles: on a separate admin hostname, reachable only from VU IP ranges (campus and VPN); administrators need a password and a second factor (an authenticator app, a passkey or a security key).
  • Everything else public is behind Caddy, with only HTTPS open.

What remains, from most to least serious:

  1. SSH on the Keycloak VM is reachable from the whole internet (found in November 2026, still to fix). The VM was created from an (extern) template, which allows SSH from anywhere. Keys-only logins make guessing useless, but SSH runs code for every connection, before any login, and serious flaws there do occur (e.g. "regreSSHion", 2024).
  2. The VU account is the real master key of a VM: whoever can log in to the SciCloud portal as its owner can take it over, regardless of SSH (step 4).
  3. Second factors can be phished: a code from an authenticator app can be typed into a fake page; a security key can't. And SSH keys are files on laptops, which malware or a thief can take.
  4. A flaw in Keycloak itself could be tried by anyone who can reach its admin console: now the whole VU network.

docs.title: 1. SSH only from the VU network
docs.text:
Allow SSH on every server only from the VU network (campus and VPN, which includes the VU SSH gateway), and keep ports 80 and 443 open to everyone. One firewall change per server: SSH only from the VU network, or setup-vm.sh --ssh-from for new VMs. This is now the default for new VMs.

TODO: apply on the Keycloak VM; check the other VMs, and the lab server (a physical server with a firewall of its own).

docs.title: 2. Security keys
docs.text:
The lab buys a set of security keys (e.g. YubiKeys), two per person with sensitive access: one to use, one as a spare in a safe place. A security key holds its secret on the device itself: it can't be copied, it only works on the real site (so it can't be phished), and it needs a touch and a PIN. Use them for:

  • SSH to the servers (below);
  • the second factor of Keycloak administrators: the master realm, and the realm admins of lab and idp. Keycloak accepts security keys as a second factor already; making them mandatory for administrators (no authenticator app) is a separate login flow. TODO: work out and test in the realm files.
  • the VU accounts of VM owners, if the VU supports security keys.

TODO: how many (two per administrator, plus a few spares), which model (with USB-C and NFC), and who keeps track of them.

SSH with a security key. OpenSSH supports security keys directly. On the admin's laptop, once per key:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O verify-required -C "<name> yubikey 1"

Give both public keys (~/.ssh/id_ed25519_sk.pub, from the key and the spare) to whoever manages the server. Once every admin of a server uses one, the server can accept nothing else, in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf:

# Only security keys, and only these accounts
PubkeyAcceptedAlgorithms sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com,sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com
AllowUsers <admin 1> <admin 2>

The console in the SciCloud portal stays the way back in when both keys are lost. (Without hardware, 1Password's SSH agent is a step up from key files: it asks for approval at every use. But anyone who gets into the 1Password account has the key.)

docs.title: 3. Keycloak up to date, quickly
docs.text:
A barrier in front of the admin console is there because of possible flaws in Keycloak. The most direct defense against those is installing security updates quickly:

  • Follow Keycloak's security announcements (the Keycloak blog, and the releases on GitHub, which can send notifications), and apply a security release within days, following Upgrading Keycloak.
  • The same for the rest of the VM: the operating system updates itself (University VMs); Caddy and PostgreSQL follow their releases.

TODO: who follows the announcements, and who updates.

docs.title: 4. Access to the VMs through the portal
docs.text:
The problem. SciCloud runs on OpenNebula. At every start, OpenNebula hands the VM its "context": settings that the one-context package in the VM applies as root, such as an SSH key, a password, and a start script that may run anything. The owner of a VM can change its context in the portal and restart it, and can open its console there (a virtual screen and keyboard), from which a restart and a changed boot command (init=/bin/bash) give a root shell. So anyone who can log in to the portal as an owner can take the VM over. Turning off root logins over SSH doesn't prevent this. (VU IT itself can always reach the VMs: that is the trust any cloud requires.)

Now:

  • Protect the VU accounts of the VM owners with a second factor, preferably a security key, and keep the number of owners small.
  • Ask VU IT whether normal users can be prevented from changing the context of a VM, and whether changes to VMs are logged.

Later, after testing on a test VM (each of these can break a VM if done wrong):

  • Turn off contextualization once a VM is set up (disable one-context), so later changes to the context do nothing. On SciCloud, the network settings often come from the context, so the network configuration must first be fixed in the VM itself, and a restart tested.
  • A password on the boot menu (GRUB), so the boot command can't be changed from the console.
  • A notification at every start of a VM, and when SSH keys change: an unexpected restart with new keys is what this attack looks like.

docs.title: Where Keycloak runs
docs.text:
An open question: is a SciCloud VM the best place for the lab's login service? What matters:

  • Who can take over the machine outside SSH: owner accounts, the console, the provider's own staff, and how well those are protected (security keys, logging).
  • Availability: when Keycloak is down, nobody in the lab can log in. Is there a support agreement, and how quickly is a failure fixed?
  • Backups and recovery by the platform itself.
  • Data location and agreements: the accounts of lab members and others are personal data; an external provider needs a data processing agreement.
  • Cost, effort, and whether VU IT accepts it.
Place Pros Cons A SciCloud VM (now) Free; VU hardware, data stays at the VU; a public address is possible Self-service portal: an owner's VU account can take the VM over (step 4); a research cloud, possibly without guaranteed availability; its own backups unclear A VM managed by VU IT (their regular hosting, not the research cloud) Run by people whose job it is; backups and monitoring by IT; probably no self-service console for owners A request process; less control over updates and configuration; possibly costs A dedicated physical server on VU premises No portal The hardware is our job (disks, failures); a remote console (IPMI) is a risk of its own. Not on the lab server, which runs many apps A VM at a European cloud provider (e.g. Hetzner, Scaleway, OVH) A provider account with a security key, snapshots, good consoles; a few euros a month Outside the VU: a data processing agreement is needed, and the VU network restrictions no longer apply by themselves Hosted Keycloak (as a service) No server of our own Costs; the provider can reach everything; less control No Keycloak of our own (the VU's login or SURF SRAM for lab) Nothing to host Considered before: no open sign-up for idp, and less control over 2FA and account recovery (Decisions)

For now, a SciCloud VM is reasonable if two things hold: the VU accounts of its owners are well protected (step 4), and VU IT confirms its availability and access rules. The most obvious alternative is a VM managed by VU IT. TODO: ask VU IT (see below).

docs.title: Further options, if needed
docs.text:
Only for when there is a concrete reason, e.g. realm admins from outside the VU (who have no VU VPN), or a request from VU IT. Each adds something to run and maintain.

  • A VPN of our own (WireGuard), on a small VM of its own. Each admin's device gets a key and an address in a private network (e.g. 10.8.0.x): traffic to that network is encrypted and sent to the VPN server's public address, which unwraps it. The admin console (and SSH) would then only accept the VPN. Without a key, the VPN doesn't answer at all, and it is easy for realm admins (switch on the app). But the keys are files on devices, with no second factor per session; it needs a UDP port that VU IT has to allow; and it is one more machine. Self-hosted tools on top of WireGuard (Headscale, NetBird) add a login with a second factor, at the cost of another service.
  • A jump host: a small VM with only SSH, the one way in to the servers (ProxyJump). Simple for technical admins; for the admin console, users need an SSH tunnel and a browser profile that uses it. A jump host and a VPN can be the same small VM.
  • Tunnel-only SSH accounts (on the Keycloak VM, or on a jump host or the lab server): an account that can only forward to the admin console, without a shell (nologin, and restrict,port-forwarding,permitopen=... on its key).
  • Tailscale: a VPN without setup; but a US company's server decides who joins, and the free plan is for 3 users. Cloudflare Tunnel: no open ports; but Cloudflare decrypts all traffic, including passwords. Client certificates: strong, but cumbersome to issue and revoke.

Whatever is chosen: never put private keys on a jump host or VPN server, and don't forward your SSH agent to it (ssh -A). With ProxyJump, the connection to a server runs from your own laptop, through the jump host, so a broken-into jump host gives no logins.

docs.title: Questions for VU IT
docs.text:
• Can normal users be prevented from changing the context of a VM, and are changes to VMs logged?
  • Is the SciCloud portal only reachable from the VU network or VPN, and do VU accounts support security keys?
  • Which address ranges are the VU network and VPN (for the SSH and admin restrictions)?
  • What availability does SciCloud offer (support, failures, backups)? And could the lab's login service run on a VM managed by VU IT instead, and who could reach its console there?

These go together with the open questions about backups (Open points).

docs.title: Our software
docs.text:
Besides running infrastructure, the lab develops open-source research software:

  • AmCAT (Amsterdam Content Analysis Toolkit): storing, managing, sharing and analysing research data.
  • AnnoTinder: annotating research data.

The lab runs its own servers of this software (Hosted services), and other research groups can host it themselves. This section only covers what matters for deploying it securely: how logins work (Authentication standard), which login provider to choose (Authentication provider), and how to move to another provider (Migration guide). Installation instructions are in the repositories of the software itself.

docs.title: Installation: apps on our servers
docs.text:
How apps are installed on the lab server and the service VMs: one system account, every app in /opt/<app> with a compose.yml at the top, and a fixed place for its data, depending on whether it must be kept. Read Docker warnings first.

The Keycloak VM follows the same layout, with its own system account keycloak instead of sal, and its folder cloned from its own repository (deploy-keycloak).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
Where What Backed up by us Deleted /opt/<app> compose.yml, .env (settings and secrets), the app's own code if we build it (src/) Yes When the app is removed /opt/<app>/data Files that must be kept Yes When the app is removed, or by the app /opt/<app>/backups Database dumps, made every day by the app's backup service Yes After 7 days (older ones stay in the nightly backup) Named volumes A database's own files, caches, models, data with a short retention No By a cleanup service or the app (short retention), or when removed

So our nightly backup of /opt (Backups) contains everything needed to restore an app: its setup, its files, and its databases (as dumps). The examples for each case are on Docker Compose standards.

For every new app, decide:

  • Files that must be kept? Mount them from ./data.
  • A database? Add the backup service (PostgreSQL, with daily backups).
  • Data that may only be kept for a limited time? A named volume with a cleanup service, or the app's own retention setting (Data with a short retention).

Record the answers in Hosted services: that is where the lab's retention policy is documented.

docs.title: 1. The system account
docs.text:
Once per server:

sudo useradd --system --home-dir /nonexistent --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin sal

For each admin, so that they can enter the app directories:

sudo usermod -aG sal <admin>

/opt stays as it is: owned by root:root, mode 755. sal is not in the docker group: membership of that group is effectively root access, and apps that run as sal without Docker would get it too (see Docker warnings). Admins run Docker with sudo.

How access works

  • Each app directory is owned by sal:sal, with mode 750. sal can change everything, admins (the sal group) can enter and read, and other users can't enter at all. That last part is what protects the files inside, whatever their own modes are.
  • Secrets in .env get mode 600, so only sal can read them. Admins use sudo when they need to.

Rules for admins

  • Everything inside /opt/<app> is done as sal: sudo -u sal <command>, or sudo -u sal bash for longer work. The exception is Docker: sudo docker compose ..., from the folder with the compose file.
  • Edit files with sudoedit -u sal <file>. It opens your own editor with your own settings, and saves the file as sal.
    • Choose the editor in your ~/.bashrc: export SUDO_EDITOR=nvim (or nano).
    • Don't run the editor as sal (sudo -u sal nvim): sal has no home directory for the editor's own files.
  • Pasting into a file on the server: go into insert mode and use your terminal's paste shortcut: Cmd+V on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+V on Linux, Ctrl+V or right-click in Windows Terminal or PuTTY. ("+p doesn't work: a server has no clipboard.)
  • Never use plain sudo for other commands inside an app directory, or files end up owned by root.
  • After copying files in from elsewhere, fix the owner: sudo chown -R sal:sal /opt/<app>.
  • Never run docker compose down -v or docker volume prune unless you mean to delete the app's volumes (with its database, caches and data with a short retention).

docs.title: 2. Adding an app
docs.text:
1. Create its directory, as an admin:

    sudo mkdir /opt/<app>

    sudo chown sal:sal /opt/<app> && sudo chmod 750 /opt/<app>

  2. Write its compose.yml, with sudoedit -u sal /opt/<app>/compose.yml, from the examples on Docker Compose standards. Our own code goes in /opt/<app>/src (sudo -u sal git clone <repo> /opt/<app>/src; a private repository needs a deploy key, a read-only SSH key for that repository, for sal).

  3. Settings and secrets go in /opt/<app>/.env, readable only by sal:

    sudo -u sal chmod 600 /opt/<app>/.env

  4. Files that must be kept: create data as sal before the first start (Docker would create it owned by root):

    sudo -u sal mkdir /opt/<app>/data

  5. Check the ports: only on 127.0.0.1 ("127.0.0.1:<port>:<port>"), and not yet taken (sudo ss -tlnp).

  6. Start it:

    cd /opt/<app> && sudo docker compose up -d

    Check that nothing is published to the outside: sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}' should show no 0.0.0.0: or [::]:. With a database: check that the first dump is in backups/.

  7. Make it reachable through Caddy: on the lab server, see Adding a service.

  8. Record it in Hosted services: what it keeps, and for how long.

docs.title: Sorting an app's data
docs.text:
Most apps don't say what they keep where. Before the first real use:

  1. Find out what it writes where: in the app's documentation, in its own example compose file (the volumes:), and by trying it: after a test run, sudo docker diff <container> lists every file the container changed outside its volumes.
  2. Sort every folder:
    • settings, accounts, uploads that must be kept: ./data;
    • a database: a named volume, plus the backup service;
    • caches and downloaded models: a named volume;
    • uploads and results that may only be kept for a limited time: a named volume with a cleanup service.

  3. Mount each folder where it belongs. A mount can point at a folder inside another mount; the more specific one wins. So the uploads can expire while the rest of the app's data is kept:

    volumes:
  - ./data:/app/data                 # settings: kept, backed up
  - uploads:/app/data/uploads        # only the uploads: deleted by the cleanup service

    (Docker leaves an empty uploads folder in data, where the second mount is attached; leave it.)

Where sorting by folder doesn't work:

  • Settings and uploads in the same folder (e.g. settings.json next to job-123.wav): no mount can separate them.
  • Folders that vary, e.g. /app/data/<user>/uploads: a mount needs a fixed path.
  • Files moved from one mount to the other: some apps write a file elsewhere first and then move it into the uploads folder. Depending on how the app moves it, that is a copy (fine) or fails with "cross-device link". A test run shows it.
  • The app keeps a list of its files (e.g. a history of transcriptions in its database): after the cleanup, the list points to files that are gone, which can confuse it.

Then use the app's own retention setting, or delete through the app (its API or admin page, run on a schedule). That is work per app: record how in Hosted services.

docs.title: Updating and removing an app
docs.text:
Updating: change the version in compose.yml (after reading the release notes), then:

cd /opt/<app> && sudo docker compose pull && sudo docker compose up -d

For our own code: sudo -u sal git -C /opt/<app>/src pull, then sudo docker compose up -d --build.

Removing (this deletes its data, so check first that it is no longer needed, following the retention rules of the privacy statement):

cd /opt/<app> && sudo docker compose down -v

sudo rm -r /opt/<app>

-v also removes its named volumes. Its folder stays in the nightly backups until they expire (up to 6 months).

docs.title: Installation: backups
docs.text:
The lab's servers are backed up in two layers (why: Backup strategies):

  1. Server backups, by VU IT: a copy of each whole server, the last resort after losing a server. TODO: confirm with VU IT which servers they back up, how often, and how long they keep the backups.
  2. Our own backups, per app: every night, each server backs up /opt, encrypted. Everything needed to restore an app is there: its compose.yml and .env, its files (data/) and its databases as dumps (backups/), made every day by the app itself (Apps on our servers). This page is about this layer.

The nightly job is in its own repository, deploy-backup, cloned to /opt/backup on every server. Every night it:

  1. checks the database dumps: every /opt/<app>/backups folder must have a dump from the last 26 hours, otherwise the app's backup service has stopped;
  2. backs up /opt with restic: encrypted on the server, before anything leaves it, and only the changes since the last backup;
  3. removes old backups: it keeps the last 7 daily, 4 weekly and 6 monthly backups, so data deleted on the server can remain in these backups for up to 6 months;
  4. checks the backups: the structure every night, and on Sundays also a sample of 5% of the data itself;
  5. reports the result to the monitoring, which emails us when a backup failed or didn't run (Monitoring).

For now, the backups stay on the server itself

Until the lab has a place for backups elsewhere, they are stored on the same server (/var/backups/restic). They protect against mistakes (a deleted file, a failed upgrade), but not against losing the server: for that, there are only the server backups of VU IT. TODO: a location off the server, to be agreed with VU IT (Changing the location).

The database server is not covered by this page yet. TODO

docs.title: Setting up a server
docs.text:
First create a check for the server in the lab's healthchecks.io project (Monitoring), and copy its ping URL. Then clone the job, and run its setup script with that URL:

sudo git clone https://github.com/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-backup.git /opt/backup

sudo /opt/backup/setup.sh https://hc-ping.com/<uuid>

The script (setup.sh) can safely run again: it never replaces a password or a repository that exists. It:

  1. makes /opt/backup readable only by root (the job must read every app's files and secrets, so it runs as root);
  2. creates the encryption password in /etc/restic/password, readable only by root;
  3. puts the ping URL in /etc/restic/env;
  4. creates the repository, where restic keeps the backups (for now /var/backups/restic);
  5. turns on the timer: every night between 03:30 and 04:00, and catching up after a night the server was off.

Store the password in the password manager

Without the password, the backups can't be read: not by us, and not by anyone else. Store it in the lab's password manager, accessible to at least two people: sudo cat /etc/restic/password.

Then make the first backup, and check it (healthchecks.io should show it too):

sudo systemctl start backup.service

journalctl -u backup.service -n 50

Updating the job later: sudo git -C /opt/backup pull. For every other restic command, use restic.sh from /opt/backup: it runs restic with this server's settings (/etc/restic/env).

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
A backup that silently stopped is the most common way to lose data. So every run reports to healthchecks.io: a ping at the start, and one with the result at the end. Healthchecks.io emails us when a run failed, and also when no run arrived for a day (e.g. the server was off, or the timer broke). It only receives these pings, no data. The free plan covers 20 checks.

For each server, in the lab's healthchecks.io project (TODO: create the account and project; who has access): add a check named after the server, with Period 1 day, Grace 2 hours, and the email addresses to notify. Its ping URL goes to setup.sh, or later in /etc/restic/env as PING_URL=<url>.

docs.title: Checking
docs.text:
• When it last ran, and when it runs next: systemctl list-timers backup.timer.
  • Whether it worked: systemctl status backup.service (status=0/SUCCESS), and the details with journalctl -u backup.service -n 50. A missing dump or unreadable files make the run fail, even though the rest is backed up.
  • The backups: sudo ./restic.sh snapshots, and what is in the latest: sudo ./restic.sh ls latest.

While there are fewer than 7 days of backups, restic keeps a few extra; that sorts itself out.

docs.title: Leaving something out
docs.text:
/etc/restic/excludes (optional, readable only by root) lists what to leave out, one pattern per line, e.g. large files in an app's folder that can be downloaded again:

/opt/<app>/models

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
From /opt/backup. Restore into a separate folder first, and copy back what you need:

sudo ./restic.sh restore latest --target /tmp/restore --include /opt/<app>/<file or folder>

The files are then in /tmp/restore/opt/<app>/.... Stop the app (sudo docker compose down, without -v), copy the files back with sudo cp -a, and start it again. An older backup: use its ID from snapshots instead of latest.

  • A database: restore its dump the same way (--include /opt/<app>/backups), and load it (Restoring a dump; Keycloak: Backups).
  • A whole app on a new server: restore /opt/<app>, and start it with sudo docker compose up -d; then load its database dump.

Test a restore after setting up the backups, and then twice a year: a backup that can't be restored is no backup.

docs.title: Changing the location
docs.text:
Once there is a place for backups elsewhere (e.g. an SFTP server or S3 storage), add it to /etc/restic/env, with what that location needs (e.g. its access keys), and create the repository there:

RESTIC_REPOSITORY=s3:https://<host>/<bucket>/<server>
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<key>
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret>

sudo ./restic.sh init

The local backups can be copied over with restic copy, or kept until they have expired.

docs.title: Installation: Docker Compose standards
docs.text:
Every app on our servers runs with Docker Compose, from a compose.yml at the top of its folder, /opt/<app>/compose.yml. One way of working, so the examples below apply everywhere, and every app's setup can be read in one file. How an app is installed (the system account, the steps): Apps on our servers.

In the app's folder What Backed up by us compose.yml The services of the app Yes .env Settings and secrets, readable only by sal Yes data/ Files that must be kept Yes backups/ Database dumps, made by the app's backup service Yes Named volumes Everything else: caches, models, a database's own files, data with a short retention No

Everything in /opt is backed up every night (Backups). The named volumes are only in the server backups of VU IT, the last resort.

Paths in a compose file (./data) count from the folder of the compose file. Docker creates a missing folder owned by root: create data/ as sal before the first start (Docker warnings). backups/ may be created by Docker: the dumps are only for root anyway.

docs.title: A basic app
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    image: example/app:1.2.3          # a fixed version, never "latest"
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: .env                    # settings and secrets
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"         # only for Caddy on this server, never "8080:8080"
  • A fixed version: upgrades happen when we change the version, after reading the release notes.
  • Ports only on 127.0.0.1: a port published without it is open to the whole internet, whatever the firewall says (Docker warnings). Services that talk to each other (an app and its database) use the compose network, without publishing a port at all.
  • Our own code: put it in /opt/<app>/src, and build it with build: ./src instead of image:.

docs.title: Files that must be kept
docs.text:
services:
  app:
    # ...
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data              # kept and backed up

Before the first start, as sal:

sudo -u sal mkdir /opt/<app>/data

If the container runs as its own user, that user must be able to write there: the app's documentation says which user (e.g. sudo chown 1000:1000 /opt/<app>/data).

docs.title: PostgreSQL, with daily backups
docs.text:
A database's own files can't be backed up while it runs: a copy can be inconsistent. So the database stays in a named volume, and a backup service in the same compose file dumps it every day into ./backups, which is backed up. It uses the official postgres image, the same version as the database, so pg_dump matches it.

services:
  app:
    # ...
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:18.7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: app
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 10

  db-backup:
    # A dump at the start and every day at 02:00 (UTC) into ./backups, kept 7 days
    image: postgres:18.7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/db-backup.sh"]
    environment:
      PGHOST: db
      PGUSER: app
      PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      PGDATABASE: app
      BACKUP_TIME: "02:00"
      KEEP_DAYS: 7
    volumes:
      - ./db-backup.sh:/db-backup.sh:ro
      - ./backups:/backups

volumes:
  db-data:

db-backup.sh, next to the compose file (the same script as in deploy-keycloak):

#!/bin/sh
# Database backup service: dumps the database once at the start, then every day at BACKUP_TIME (UTC),
# into /backups, and keeps the dumps of the last KEEP_DAYS days. Runs in the official postgres image.
# Settings: PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE (the connection), BACKUP_TIME (default 02:00),
# KEEP_DAYS (default 7), DUMP_OPTIONS (extra pg_dump options).
set -eu
umask 077
time="${BACKUP_TIME:-02:00}"
keep="${KEEP_DAYS:-7}"
hours="${time%%:*}"; minutes="${time##*:}"
at=$(( ${hours#0} * 3600 + ${minutes#0} * 60 ))   # "08" would be read as octal, so without the leading 0

dump() {
    file="/backups/$PGDATABASE-$(date -u +%Y%m%d).dump"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    if pg_dump --format=custom ${DUMP_OPTIONS:-} > "$file.partial"; then
        mv "$file.partial" "$file"
        echo "$(date -u -Iseconds) dump written: $file"
    else
        rm -f "$file.partial"
        echo "$(date -u -Iseconds) ERROR: pg_dump failed" >&2
    fi
    find /backups -name "$PGDATABASE-*.dump" -type f -mtime +"$((keep - 1))" -delete
}

until pg_isready -q; do sleep 5; done
dump
while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%s)
    next=$(( now - now % 86400 + at ))
    [ "$next" -gt "$now" ] || next=$(( next + 86400 ))
    sleep $(( next - now ))
    dump
done
  • Check it after the first start: sudo docker compose logs db-backup says dump written, and the dump is in backups/.
  • Monitoring: the server's nightly backup fails (and so sends an email) if a backups/ folder has no dump from the last 26 hours (Backups).
  • The history: the folder keeps 7 days; the nightly backup keeps older dumps for up to 6 months.

docs.title: Restoring a dump
docs.text:
This replaces the database with the dump. From the app's folder:

  1. Stop the app, so nothing writes to the database (the database itself keeps running):

    sudo docker compose stop app db-backup

  2. Choose the dump: one in backups/ (sudo ls backups/), or an older one from the nightly backup (Restoring, --include /opt/<app>/backups).

  3. Empty the database, and load the dump:

    sudo docker compose exec -T db dropdb -U app app

    sudo docker compose exec -T db createdb -U app app

    sudo cat backups/<dump> | sudo docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U app -d app --no-owner

  4. Start everything again:

    sudo docker compose up -d

Test a restore once when setting up an app, e.g. on a copy: a backup that can't be restored is no backup.

docs.title: Data with a short retention
docs.text:
Data that may only be kept for a limited time (e.g. uploaded audio and its transcripts) goes in a named volume, so it isn't in our backups, with a cleanup service in the same compose file that deletes files once they are older than the retention period:

services:
  app:
    # ...
    volumes:
      - uploads:/app/uploads          # deleted after 30 days, not backed up

  cleanup:
    # Retention: every hour, delete uploads not changed for 30 days
    image: busybox:1.37
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: >
      sh -c 'while true; do
               find /uploads -type f -mtime +30 -delete;
               find /uploads -mindepth 1 -type d -empty -delete;
               sleep 3600;
             done'
    volumes:
      - uploads:/uploads

volumes:
  uploads:
  • Only the folder for uploads and results: never a folder that also holds settings or a database. How to find out what an app writes where: Sorting an app's data.
  • -mtime +30 counts from the last change of a file: a file that is only read now and then is still deleted on time.
  • The app's own retention setting is better, if it has one: the app then also cleans up its own records. Record which applies in Hosted services, which is also where the retention policy is documented for IT and the privacy statement.
  • The server backups of VU IT do contain these volumes, for as long as IT keeps its backups. TODO: ask VU IT how long that is.
  • Test the retention with a short period first: e.g. -mmin +10 instead of -mtime +30, and check after a quarter of an hour that old files are gone and the app still works.

docs.title: Docker warnings
docs.text: Rules for running Docker containers on any of our servers: the lab server, university VMs, and the Keycloak VM. Two things about Docker are easy to get wrong, and both affect the security of the whole server.

docs.title: Published ports bypass the firewall
docs.text:
Read this before running containers

The server's firewall doesn't protect Docker containers. A port published by a container is open to the whole internet, whatever the firewall allows.

Why. A firewall on the server (iptables, ufw, or the firewall file of a university VM) filters the traffic of the server itself: incoming traffic for the server (the INPUT chain) and outgoing traffic from it (the OUTPUT chain). Traffic to and from containers is forwarded by Docker (the FORWARD chain), with its own rules, so it never passes those rules. This is how Docker works on any Linux machine (see Docker: packet filtering and firewalls).

What this means:

  • Incoming: a published port (ports: - "5432:5432" in a compose file, or docker run -p 5432:5432) is reachable from the internet, even if the firewall doesn't allow port 5432. Accidentally publishing a database port exposes the database.
  • Outgoing: containers can connect to any port on the internet, even ports that the firewall blocks for the server itself. For instance, the email relay of the Keycloak deployment can send email via SMTP on port 587 without a firewall rule.

Rules:

  1. Only publish ports that should be public, typically only 80 and 443 of a reverse proxy (Caddy). Let containers talk to each other over Docker networks, without publishing ports. The Keycloak installation works this way: only Caddy publishes ports, and the database is on an internal network without internet access.
  2. If a port should only be reachable from the server itself (e.g. an app behind a Caddy that runs on the server, as on the lab server, or a database tool), publish it on the loopback address: "127.0.0.1:5432:5432" instead of "5432:5432".

  3. Check which ports are published, after every change:

    sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'

    Anything with 0.0.0.0: or [::]: in front of the port is reachable from the internet.

  4. Restricting published ports (e.g. to the university network) is done in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain, not in the server's own firewall rules. Prefer restricting access in the reverse proxy instead, as the Keycloak deployment does for its admin console.

docs.title: The docker group is root access
docs.text:
Run Docker with sudo, and don't add anyone to the docker group: not admins, and not the system accounts that own the files of an app (keycloak, sal). Anyone who can run Docker can mount the whole disk into a container, so membership of the docker group is effectively root access, without the logging that sudo gives. A program that runs as a system account in the docker group (e.g. an app without Docker, run by systemd as sal) would have that access too.

Files are still owned by a system account; only the docker compose commands use sudo. See Apps on our servers and the Keycloak installation (Users and permissions).

docs.title: Directories for bind mounts
docs.text: When a bind mount (e.g. ./data:/data in a compose file) points to a directory that doesn't exist, Docker creates it, owned by root. Create such directories yourself before the first start, as the account that owns the app (e.g. sudo -u sal mkdir /opt/<app>/data).

docs.title: Installation: Keycloak VM
docs.text:
This guide sets up the lab's login service: Keycloak on a single VM, with PostgreSQL and Caddy (TLS via Let's Encrypt), using the files in the repository deploy-keycloak, cloned to /opt/keycloak. It takes about an hour. What the result looks like (the hostnames, the realms, how users log in, and the security measures): Keycloak VM. What was tested: the test checklist.

The admin hostname

The admin hostname is not published: replace <admin hostname> with it. The IP ranges and the secrets are only on the VM (in .env and caddy/admin-access.caddy).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Component Role Caddy Public TLS certificates via Let's Encrypt. Forwards only the paths that need to be public to Keycloak, over a second TLS connection (re-encrypt). Built with a rate limit module, to limit requests that make Keycloak send emails. Keycloak An optimized image (built from the official image), started with start --optimized. Creates the realms from realms/ when it starts, if they don't exist yet. Only accepts HTTPS, with an internal certificate (valid for 10 years) that only Caddy trusts. tls-init A one-off service that creates the internal certificate on the first start (and does nothing on later starts). PostgreSQL The database, only reachable by Keycloak. mail-relay Sends all email of the realms to the email provider; the only place with the provider's password (step 7).

The two hostnames: auth.societal-analytics.nl (public: /realms/, /resources/ and /.well-known/; everything else returns 404) and the admin hostname (the admin consoles, the admin API and the master realm; restricted to the VPN in step 4).

File Contents compose.yml The services, pinned versions, memory limits, health checks, and two networks (the database network has no internet access) Dockerfile The optimized Keycloak image (kc.sh build with PostgreSQL and health endpoints) Caddy.Dockerfile Caddy with the rate limit module realms/ The realms (master, lab, idp) as Keycloak realm files, imported when a realm doesn't exist yet (step 7); realms/README.md explains what we changed check-realms.py Checks realms/ for mistakes that Keycloak accepts silently (run it after every change) themes/ Our look and texts for the login pages, the account console and emails (logo, colours, the texts for lab members), mounted into Keycloak (Themes); themes/README.md lists them internal-tls.sh Creates the internal certificate (run by the tls-init service) admin-cli.sh Runs Keycloak's admin command-line tool (kcadm.sh) inside the container, over the internal TLS connection caddy/ Everything for Caddy, mounted into its container: caddy/Caddyfile The public and admin hostnames, and the email limits caddy/admin-access.example.caddy The template for the local Caddy setting caddy/admin-access.caddy (copied in step 2, never committed): the restrictions of the admin hostname (step 4). caddy/init.sh Run by the caddy-init service before Caddy starts: creates caddy/admin-access.caddy from its template if it is missing, so that Caddy can always start .env.example All settings. Copied to .env, which holds the secrets and is never committed. db-backup.sh The db-backup service: a daily database dump into backups/ (step 9)

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
The VM. On a university VM, first follow Installation: university VMs: secure SSH logins, open ports 80 and 443 in the VM firewall, and install Docker. Read the warning there about Docker bypassing the VM firewall.

DNS. Create two A records pointing to the VM's IPv4 address, auth and the admin hostname. Don't create AAAA (IPv6) records: with IPv4 only, the IP restriction of the admin hostname only needs IPv4 ranges, and Let's Encrypt can't fail on a stale IPv6 address. If your DNS provider can proxy traffic (e.g. Cloudflare), use "DNS only", otherwise Caddy can't see visitors' IP addresses. Check from your own machine:

dig +short auth.societal-analytics.nl

Ports. Ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from the internet (Let's Encrypt needs port 80), and nothing else on the VM may use them. Check on the VM:

sudo ss -tlnp '( sport = :80 or sport = :443 )'

Only a header line, without any rows below it, means the ports are free. This doesn't show whether they are reachable from outside: that shows in step 2, when Caddy obtains its certificates.

Docker. Docker Engine with the compose plugin (installation). This guide runs Docker with sudo (see Users and permissions).

sudo docker compose version

docs.title: Users and permissions
docs.text:
The deployment uses two accounts:

Account Role Rights keycloak (system user) Owns the files in /opt/keycloak, including .env with the secrets No login shell, no sudo, not in the docker group Your own admin account (your personal account on the VM) Runs the commands in this guide sudo, and member of the keycloak group

How commands are run:

  • File operations (cloning, editing .env, git pull) run as keycloak, with sudo -u keycloak ..., so that the files stay owned by keycloak.
  • Docker commands (docker compose ..., ./admin-cli.sh) run from your own account with sudo, from /opt/keycloak. Docker reads .env as root, so your account doesn't need to be able to read it.

Required: your admin account must be in the keycloak group

/opt/keycloak is only accessible to the keycloak user and group (chmod 750). The Docker commands are run from it, so your admin account must be a member of the keycloak group, otherwise cd into the folder fails with Permission denied. Group membership gives access to the folder and the deployment files, but not to .env, which stays readable only by keycloak (chmod 600).

Why not simpler:

  • Don't add keycloak (or anyone) to the docker group. Membership of the docker group is effectively root access: anyone who can run Docker can mount the whole disk into a container. Running Docker with sudo keeps that power with administrators, and sudo logs who did what.
  • Don't give keycloak sudo rights. That would turn the service account into an admin account.
  • The containers don't run as the keycloak host user: Keycloak runs as its own user inside its container. The host user only owns the files.

docs.title: System user and folder
docs.text:
Create the keycloak system user and group, with /opt/keycloak as its home folder:

sudo groupadd --system keycloak

sudo useradd --system -g keycloak --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --home-dir /opt/keycloak keycloak

sudo mkdir /opt/keycloak && sudo chown keycloak:keycloak /opt/keycloak && sudo chmod 750 /opt/keycloak

Add your own admin account to the keycloak group:

sudo usermod -aG keycloak "$USER"

Log out and log in again, so that the group membership takes effect. Then check that keycloak is listed in your groups, and that you can open the folder:

id

ls /opt/keycloak

docs.title: Files and settings
docs.text:
Get the files onto the VM, as keycloak, into the (still empty) folder:

sudo -u keycloak git clone https://github.com/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-keycloak.git /opt/keycloak

All further commands in this guide are run from here:

cd /opt/keycloak

Create .env, readable only by keycloak:

sudo -u keycloak cp .env.example .env && sudo -u keycloak chmod 600 .env

Generate two secrets with the command below (run it once per secret), and paste them into .env: POSTGRES_PASSWORD and INTERNAL_TLS_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD.

openssl rand -hex 32

The password of the temporary admin (KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD) must meet the password policy of the master realm (an uppercase letter and a digit); generate it with:

echo "Temp-$(openssl rand -hex 24)"

Fill in the other values in .env: the two hostnames (without https://), ACME_EMAIL (for Let's Encrypt expiry notices), and the values under "Realms": the email provider and the Google and GitHub apps (see step 7). Keycloak creates the realms on its first start, with these values, and doesn't start while one is missing. Store the secrets in your password manager as well.

sudo -u keycloak nano .env

Create the local Caddy setting caddy/admin-access.caddy from its template: it restricts the admin hostname (step 4). The copy is not in the repository, so git pull never changes it.

sudo -u keycloak cp caddy/admin-access.example.caddy caddy/admin-access.caddy

Set up the admin restriction now, so the admin hostname is restricted from the first start: find your IP ranges and edit caddy/admin-access.caddy as described in step 4.

If the file is missing when the stack starts, it is created from the template (Caddy doesn't start without it): unchanged, the template adds no admin restriction.

docs.title: Build and start
docs.text:
From your own account, in the deployment folder. The first time, this builds the Keycloak image, and the tls-init service creates the internal certificate:

sudo docker compose up -d --build

Wait until Keycloak is healthy (about a minute):

sudo docker compose ps

On this first start, Keycloak also creates the realms from realms/ (step 7).

Check that Caddy obtained the certificates (look for certificate obtained successfully):

sudo docker compose logs caddy | grep -i certificate

docs.title: 3. Point the admin realm to the admin hostname
docs.text:
The login pages of the master realm (used by the admin console) must be on the admin hostname: the public hostname blocks them. On a new installation this is already done: master-realm.json sets the frontend URL of master to KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN. Check it (it should show the admin hostname):

curl -s https://<admin hostname>/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration | grep -o '"issuer":"[^"]*"'

On an installation from before the realm files, or after changing the admin hostname, set it directly in the database (see Changing the hostnames).

docs.title: 4. Restrict admin access
docs.text:
Keycloak recommends not exposing the administration interfaces to the public internet, and in particular restricting the administrative master realm to internal access (see Configuring Keycloak for production and the exposed path recommendations). With this step, everything on the admin hostname (the admin consoles, the admin API and the master realm) is only reachable from the IP ranges you choose, e.g. the university network and its VPN. The public hostname, where users log in, is not affected.

How it works. The admin hostname reads the rules in caddy/admin-access.caddy (copied from caddy/admin-access.example.caddy in step 2), from top to bottom; the first rule that matches a request decides. Requests that match no rule go to Keycloak. The file is local to the VM: it is not in the repository, so git pull never changes it.

Set this up before the first start (step 2), so the admin hostname is never open; you can also do it later. After a change while Caddy runs, apply it with a reload, which checks the file first: if it contains a mistake, the reload fails with an error message, and Caddy keeps running with the previous settings.

sudo docker compose exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile

docs.title: Find your IP ranges
docs.text:
Run this on your own device (not on the VM), connected to the VPN:

curl -4 https://ifconfig.me

Then look up the range that address belongs to (the whois port is blocked on some networks; this uses HTTPS):

curl -s https://rdap.db.ripe.net/ip/<your IP> | grep -E '"(name|startAddress|endAddress)"'

Check that name belongs to your institution, and write the range in CIDR notation. This command calculates it from startAddress and endAddress:

python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; print(*i.summarize_address_range(i.ip_address('START'), i.ip_address('END')))"

For example, 192.0.2.0 to 192.0.2.255 is 192.0.2.0/24. The VPN and the campus network may use different ranges: repeat this on campus without VPN (wired and Wi-Fi) if you also want access from there, and list every range you find. The university's IT department can tell you the official ranges. A whole institutional range includes everyone on that network: it is an extra layer, admin accounts still need 2FA.

docs.title: Restrict the admin hostname
docs.text:
Edit the file (in step 2, or later):

sudo -u keycloak nano caddy/admin-access.caddy

At the bottom, remove the # in front of the restriction, and put your ranges after remote_ip, separated by spaces:

@not_allowed not remote_ip 192.0.2.0/24 198.51.100.0/24
handle @not_allowed {
    respond 403
}

If Caddy is already running, apply it with the reload above. Check, from your own device (once the stack runs). On the VPN this shows the master realm's issuer; without the VPN (e.g. on a phone hotspot) it should return 403:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<admin hostname>/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration

docs.title: Exceptions for specific realms
docs.text:
The idp realm gets no exception: its users never need the admin console, and its clients are managed by our own admins.

A realm can have admins who are not on your network, e.g. a research group outside the university that manages its own realm (see Isolated OIDC providers). For such a realm, add an exception above the restriction, in the same file. It makes the admin console of that realm, and only that realm, reachable from another range (or from anywhere, without the remote_ip line):

@realm_research_group {
    path /admin/research-group/* /admin/realms/research-group /admin/realms/research-group/* /admin/serverinfo /resources/*
    remote_ip 203.0.113.0/24
}
handle @realm_research_group {
    import keycloak
}
  • Replace research-group with the name of the realm (four times), and use a unique name after @ for each exception (letters, digits and underscores).
  • The paths are what a realm's admin console needs: its console, the admin API for that realm, general server information (/admin/serverinfo, behind login), and scripts and styles (/resources/).
  • The master realm and the other realms stay restricted: their paths are not part of the exception. Admins of the realm can only manage their own realm.
  • Admins of such a realm have an account in that realm with the role realm-admin of the client realm-management (in that realm: Users → the user → Role mapping → Assign role → filter by clients). They use the console at https://<admin hostname>/admin/<realm>/console/. Make 2FA required for them in that realm.
  • Apply it with sudo docker compose exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.

Tested: with the restriction and an exception, the realm's admin console works from the exception range, while the master realm, the console of another realm, and the admin API of other realms are refused (by Caddy, and by Keycloak for the realm admin's own token).

docs.title: 5. Checks
docs.text:
From your own device (on an allowed network, if you restricted admin access in step 4):

curl -s https://<admin hostname>/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration | grep -o '"issuer":"[^"]*"'

This should show https://<admin hostname>/realms/master. Then check that the public hostname doesn't expose the admin console or the admin realm (both should return 404):

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/admin/

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration

docs.title: 6. Permanent admin account
docs.text:
Following Bootstrapping and recovering an admin account: the bootstrap account is temporary, and must be replaced by a permanent admin with 2FA. The master realm is for administrators only; users never go in master.

  1. Open https://<admin hostname>/admin/ (from an allowed network, if you restricted admin access) and log in as temp-admin. Because 2FA is mandatory in master, Keycloak first asks you to set up an authenticator app and recovery codes for temp-admin too (it is deleted in step 6). A yellow banner then says you are using a temporary admin account.
  2. In the master realm, go to Users → Add user. Fill in your email address (it is the username), turn on Email verified, and under Required user actions choose Configure OTP. Click Create.
  3. On the Credentials tab, click Set password, and turn off Temporary.
  4. On the Role mapping tab, click Assign role, filter by realm roles, and assign admin.
  5. Open a private browser window, go to the admin console, and log in as the new admin. Keycloak shows Mobile Authenticator Setup: scan the QR code with an authenticator app. Then it shows Recovery Authentication Codes: save them somewhere safe (e.g. a password manager), apart from the authenticator app. Check that you can use the admin console.
  6. As the new admin, go to Users, and delete temp-admin.
  7. Remove the value of KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env. It is only used on the very first start, but there is no reason to keep it.

By default, Keycloak asks for the second factor of every user who has one configured, so the permanent admin always needs their authenticator app.

docs.title: 7. Realms
docs.text:
The realms are in realms/ as complete Keycloak realm files (master-realm.json, lab-realm.json, idp-realm.json). Keycloak imports them itself when it starts (its own --import-realm), but only realms that don't exist yet: an existing realm is never changed. So the files set up the realms once, document how they are configured (realms/README.md explains what we changed), and make it easy to set them up again. Later changes are made in the admin console.

Realm For Login Registration External login master Administrators only Password + mandatory 2FA No No (and no email) lab The lab's own infrastructure Password + mandatory 2FA Added by us (Adding lab members) No (institutional addresses) idp The login for the lab's own servers (AmCAT, AnnoTinder, and more) Password + optional 2FA Open: an account gives no access by itself Google, GitHub

In all realms:

  • 2FA: OTP (authenticator app), passkeys or security keys, and recovery codes count as a second factor. Users can also sign in with only a passkey ("Sign in with Passkey" on the login page), which counts as 2FA, also where 2FA is mandatory. With mandatory 2FA, users without a second factor are asked to set up OTP when they log in. After setting up OTP, users set up recovery codes. In idp, Google and GitHub replace only the password: the second factor is asked after them, in the same way. All login paths, and why: How users log in.
  • Forgot password, or first time (lab, idp): after the email link (valid 30 minutes), users with a second factor enter it, then choose a new password, and are logged in. The email link never replaces the second factor. In lab, users without a second factor set one up in the same go.
  • The amr claim in tokens contains mfa when a second factor was used, and pwd for a password (for our software: OIDC_MFA_CLAIM=amr:mfa, see the Authentication standard).
  • Passwords: at least 10 characters, with an uppercase letter and a digit, not equal to the username or email.
  • Login action timeout 30 minutes for each page of the login (e.g. setting up 2FA, saving the recovery codes), brute force detection, and login and admin events kept for 90 days.
  • Sessions at Keycloak last 30 minutes in idp (applications keep their own sessions), and up to 8 hours in master. In lab, a session ends after 2 hours without activity, and lasts at most 10 hours: the lab login on the lab server checks it regularly, so this is how long members stay signed in to the lab's services (Lab server). In lab, Remember me on the login page keeps users logged in on that device for up to 30 days (7 days idle).
  • The email address is the username, and users log in with it. In lab and idp, users change their address in the account console (Personal info → Update email): the address, and with it the username, only changes after they confirm the new address with a link sent to it. The user stays the same (same sub), also for users who log in with Google or GitHub. In master, which has no email server, admins change an address in the admin console. Existing usernames without an email address (temp-admin, a recovery admin) keep working.
  • Registration (in idp) asks only for email and name: users choose their password after verifying their email address. This is Keycloak's default when email verification is on, so that nobody can set a password for an address they don't own.

The files contain no users, signing keys or IDs: Keycloak creates those. Values from .env are placeholders (${SMTP_FROM}, ${IDP_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}, ...); Keycloak doesn't start while one of them is missing (Missing in .env: ... in its log).

docs.title: Google and GitHub (idp realm)
docs.text:
The idp realm offers login with Google and GitHub. The lab realm doesn't: its accounts are tied to institutional email addresses (institutional login may be added later). Register an OAuth app at both, with this redirect URI (callback URL):

https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/idp/broker/<google or github>/endpoint
  • Google: in the Google Cloud console, Create credentials → OAuth client ID → Web application, with the redirect URI above. The OAuth consent screen needs the scopes openid, email and profile, and must be published (In production), otherwise only test users can log in.
  • GitHub: under the organization's Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps → New OAuth App, with the redirect URI above as Authorization callback URL. Email addresses from GitHub are not trusted as verified: Keycloak verifies them itself.

Put the client IDs and secrets in .env (IDP_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, IDP_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, IDP_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, IDP_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET). The import stores the secrets in Keycloak's database. The admin console never shows them, and Keycloak only sends a secret to the provider it was entered for: an admin who changes where a provider points must enter the secret again.

docs.title: Email: the relay
docs.text:
All email of the lab and idp realms goes through the email relay (mail-relay, a Postfix container), which sends it on to the email provider. master has no email: admin access never depends on an inbox.

  • Only the relay has the provider's password. Keycloak sends to the relay without a password, and only Keycloak can reach the relay (on its own internal network). A realm admin who points the realm's email settings elsewhere gets no password.
  • Only one sender address: the relay refuses emails from any other address than SMTP_FROM.
  • A cap for the whole Keycloak instance: at most EMAIL_RELAY_LIMIT emails per EMAIL_RELAY_LIMIT_PERIOD (default 400 per hour). Above it, the relay refuses emails until the period ends, and users see an error that the email could not be sent. It protects the monthly quota of the email provider; see Email limits. Apply a change with sudo docker compose up -d mail-relay.
  • Queueing: when the provider is unreachable, the relay keeps the emails and retries.

Fill in SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASSWORD, SMTP_FROM and SMTP_FROM_NAME in .env. The relay requires TLS to the provider: use port 587 (STARTTLS). For Scaleway Transactional Email: host smtp.tem.scaleway.com, user your Scaleway project ID, and as password an API secret key with only the permission to send email.

Check the relay's log (each email shows up with status=sent, or the reason it wasn't):

sudo docker compose logs mail-relay

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Keycloak's log shows the import on the first start (Realm 'lab' imported, ...; on later starts: already exists. Import skipped):

sudo docker compose logs keycloak | grep -i import

Then check, in a private browser window:

  • the idp login page (https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/idp/account) shows Google and GitHub, and the lab login page doesn't;
  • a user without a second factor is asked to set up OTP in lab, and not in idp;
  • Realm settings → Email → Test connection works in both realms, and the email shows up in sudo docker compose logs mail-relay.

docs.title: Setting up a realm again
docs.text:
To set up lab or idp again from its file (e.g. after experiments, or to get the latest version of the file): make a backup (Backups), delete the realm in the admin console (Manage realms → the realm → Action → Delete; this deletes its users too), and restart Keycloak:

sudo docker compose restart keycloak

After setting up idp again, create the clients of our deployments again (step 8), with their new secrets. master is only imported on a new installation: on an existing one, it keeps its settings.

Changes to the realm files after the realms were created only reach a new realm. (For lab, the latest change is its session times: Realm settings → Sessions → SSO Session Idle 2 hours, SSO Session Max 10 hours, which can be set by hand instead.) For lab and idp without users, set them up again as above. master keeps its settings. It still works with a password and a second factor; to bring it in line with the files by hand, in the admin console of master:

  • Recovery codes after OTP setup: Authentication → Required actions → Configure OTP, the gear icon, turn on Add Recovery Codes.
  • Login action timeout: Realm settings → Sessions → Login action timeout: 30 minutes.
  • Passkey login (optional; it takes more steps, see realms/README.md): admins can do without it, and master gets it on a new installation.
Upgrading an installation from before November 2026

Updating from the version with the app registration site: after git pull, remove its container with sudo docker compose up -d --remove-orphans, delete caddy/email-tiers.caddy, and remove APPS_HOSTNAME, APP_REGISTRATION_CLIENT_SECRET, APP_REGISTRATION_SESSION_SECRET, MAX_APPS_PER_USER and CONTACT_EMAIL from .env, and the DNS record of the apps hostname. Set up idp again (above): this removes the site's client and service account, and adds the client policy of step 8.

Updating from the version with keycloak-config-cli: the keycloak-config client in master is no longer used, and it has admin rights: delete it (Clients → keycloak-config → Action → Delete), and remove KEYCLOAK_CONFIG_SECRET from .env. If lab and idp have no users yet, delete them and restart Keycloak to set them up from the files, as above. (From the version with a vault, also: put the SMTP password in .env as SMTP_PASSWORD, the idp client secrets as IDP_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET and IDP_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, set SMTP_PORT=587, and delete the vault/ folder.)

docs.title: Changing the realm files
docs.text:
The files are the starting point and the documentation; the realms themselves are changed in the admin console. To keep a change in the files too:

  • Small changes: edit the file directly, and run the checks:

    python3 check-realms.py

    It catches mistakes in flows that Keycloak accepts silently, e.g. a "Condition - sub-flow executed" that refers to a flow that doesn't exist (which happens when a flow is copied in the admin console: the copy keeps the old name), and placeholders that compose.yml doesn't pass to Keycloak. * New values from .env: write ${NAME} (upper case), and add NAME to the environment of the keycloak service in compose.yml. Lower-case placeholders, e.g. ${role_admin}, are Keycloak's own texts. * Larger changes: make them in the admin console of a test installation, and export the realm (Realm settings → Action → Partial export, with clients, groups and roles). Then put the placeholders back for the secrets and hostnames, and compare with the old file before replacing it.

docs.title: 8. Clients for our deployments
docs.text:
Each AmCAT or AnnoTinder server of the lab (and anything else that logs in with idp) is a client in the idp realm. AmCAT and AnnoTinder on the same host share one client, so users consent once per host. Create it in the admin console of idp:

  1. Clients → Create client. Client ID: the host, e.g. amcat-example-org. Name: shown to users on the consent screen, e.g. "AmCAT (example.org)". Next.
  2. Client authentication: on. Authentication flow: only Standard flow. Next.
  3. Valid redirect URIs: the exact callback URL of the server (see its documentation), e.g. https://amcat.example.org/api/auth/callback: https://, no wildcards (*). Valid post logout redirect URIs: + (the same as the redirect URIs). Don't leave this field empty: Keycloak refuses an empty value. Save.
  4. Credentials tab: copy the Client secret.
  5. Configure the server: OIDC_HOST=https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/idp, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM=amr:mfa (see the Authentication standard). Our software requests the scopes openid email.

A new client gets the scopes email (address and whether it is verified), amr (2FA), and the basics (sub, auth_time), and profile (the name) only when it asks for it; no roles. Users see that on the consent screen: "This app will be able to: see your email address; see whether you signed in with two-factor authentication", and "see your name" for a service that requests profile. Other services (not ours) work the same way: they often request openid profile email.

The client policy deployment-clients (in realms/idp-realm.json) applies to every confidential client that an admin creates or changes in idp. It prevents mistakes, not misuse (an admin can change the policy):

  • Consent is turned on automatically: users see the client's name before it gets their name and email address.
  • PKCE (S256) is turned on automatically, and required at every login: a login request without PKCE is refused (our software always uses it).
  • Redirect URIs with http://, wildcards or other unsafe forms are refused, with "Invalid Redirect Uri". Local development doesn't need a client: our software has a development mode.

Tested on a test installation: a client created step by step as above gets consent and PKCE; a wildcard redirect URI is refused; a login without PKCE is refused, with PKCE it shows the consent screen and gives tokens. Keycloak's own clients (e.g. the account console, which is public) are not affected.

docs.title: 9. Backups
docs.text:
The VM is backed up like every server (Backups): every night, /opt (with .env, caddy/admin-access.caddy and the database dumps) is backed up, encrypted. Set that up after this guide.

The database itself is dumped by the db-backup service in compose.yml: at its start, and every day at 02:00 (UTC), into /opt/keycloak/backups/keycloak-<date>.dump, kept for 7 days. It starts with the rest. Check it after the first start:

sudo docker compose logs db-backup
  • The dumps are sensitive: they contain user data, password hashes, client secrets and the realm signing keys. They are only readable by root, and the backups are encrypted.
  • Keycloak has no master key: a dump, plus .env and caddy/admin-access.caddy, is all you need to restore. The internal certificate is not needed: on a new VM, tls-init creates a new one.
  • Keycloak's register of running instances (the jgroups_ping table) is left out of the dump. Restoring old entries would make Keycloak believe another instance is running.

Restore (tested; this replaces the current database). Choose a dump in backups/, or an older one from the nightly backup (Restoring, --include /opt/keycloak/backups). Then:

cd /opt/keycloak

sudo docker compose stop keycloak db-backup

sudo docker compose exec -T postgres dropdb -U keycloak keycloak

sudo docker compose exec -T postgres createdb -U keycloak keycloak

sudo cat backups/<dump> | sudo docker compose exec -T postgres pg_restore -U keycloak -d keycloak --no-owner

sudo docker compose up -d

Do a restore test after setting up the backups, e.g. on a test machine.

docs.title: 10. Maintenance
docs.text:
Logs:

sudo docker compose logs -f keycloak

A warning about deprecated features (identity-brokering-api:v1, twitter-broker:v1) being enabled by default is expected.

The internal certificate is valid for 10 years. Check its expiry date (shown in the output of tls-init):

sudo docker compose logs tls-init

To replace it (e.g. before it expires), create a new one, and restart Keycloak and Caddy so that both use it:

sudo docker compose run --rm tls-init renew

sudo docker compose restart keycloak caddy

Upgrading Keycloak. Keycloak has quarterly feature releases and frequent patch releases; follow the Keycloak blog for releases and security announcements.

  1. Read the release notes and the upgrading guide for the new version.
  2. Make a backup: sudo systemctl start backup.service (then check it with journalctl -u backup.service -n 20).
  3. Change the version in compose.yml (KEYCLOAK_IMAGE, the only place where it is set). Preferably make the change in the repository, and get it onto the VM with sudo -u keycloak git pull.
  4. Rebuild and restart. Keycloak migrates the database on start.
sudo docker compose build --pull && sudo docker compose up -d

PostgreSQL: change the image tag in compose.yml, and run sudo docker compose up -d. Minor PostgreSQL versions (e.g. 18.7 to 18.8) need nothing else. A new major version (e.g. 18 to 19) needs a dump and restore; check that Keycloak supports it first.

Caddy is built with the rate limit module: change CADDY_VERSION in Caddy.Dockerfile (and, if needed, the pinned commit of the module), then rebuild with sudo docker compose up -d --build caddy.

The realm files stay importable after a Keycloak upgrade: Keycloak converts older realm files when it imports them. After a major upgrade, set up a test realm from the files once to check.

docs.title: Email limits
docs.text:
Keycloak has no limit on the emails it sends. Without limits, anyone could use the registration and "forgot password" forms to send many emails: to bomb someone's inbox, or to use up the monthly quota of the email provider (after which nobody gets a verification or reset email until the next month). There are two limits:

Limit Where Default Counts Above the limit Per IP address Caddy; .env: EMAIL_LIMIT_PER_IP per EMAIL_LIMIT_PER_IP_WINDOW 200 per hour Requests that can send an email, plus registrations and first logins with Google or GitHub That person sees "Too many attempts from your network" All email The relay; .env: EMAIL_RELAY_LIMIT per EMAIL_RELAY_LIMIT_PERIOD 400 per hour Emails actually sent Keycloak can't send email; users see that the email could not be sent

The requests that can send an email are the first visit to the "verify your email" page (after registering, or when a user with an unverified email address logs in) and submitting "forgot password". Logins (with password, OTP, passkey, Google or GitHub), token requests and refresh grants, and choosing the new password after the email link are never limited. (Users with a second factor enter it on the reset page after the link, which counts once more: a reset counts 1, or 2 with a second factor.)

How they count:

  • Caddy (per IP): a sliding window. A request is allowed if fewer than the maximum were allowed in the last period, so spots free up one by one, each exactly one period after the request that took it. Refused requests are not counted, so trying again doesn't make the wait longer. The error page sends the wait time as Retry-After.
  • The relay (all email): a fixed period. The count starts at the first email and is reset when the period ends. Above the cap, all email is refused until then (from seconds to the whole period), after which the full number is available again. Refused emails are not queued: users have to try again.
  • Why the limit on all email is only in the relay: Caddy counts requests, and anyone can send requests that make Keycloak send nothing (e.g. reloading a page, or invalid requests). A limit on all requests together in Caddy could be used up by one person, and would block sign-ups for everyone. The relay only counts emails that were actually sent, which one person can't do in large numbers, because of the limit per IP address. So the cap on all email is only reached by an attack from many addresses, or by email that doesn't pass Caddy (e.g. emails that admins trigger).

Choosing the numbers:

  • All email protects the provider's monthly quota (check it in the provider's console; for Scaleway under the project's quotas). Keep the cap well below it: an attack that keeps going sends at most the cap per period, e.g. 400 × 24 = 9,600 per day. Set up a usage alert at the provider (e.g. at half the monthly quota) if it offers one: an attack that stays below the cap is only visible in the usage, and in the logs below.
  • Per IP address is generous, because many people can share one address (e.g. a class on a campus network): 200 per hour is about 100 sign-ups per hour from one address. It must stay well below the cap on all email, so that one address can't use that up.

Is a limit being hit? Caddy logs every refused request, with the limit (zone) and the IP address (key), and the relay logs every refused email:

sudo docker compose logs caddy | grep 'rate limit exceeded'

sudo docker compose logs mail-relay | grep -E 'rate limit exceeded|reject'

The counts are kept in memory: a restart of Caddy or the relay resets them (a Caddy reload doesn't).

docs.title: Adding lab members
docs.text:
lab has no registration form: only people we add can use it. We add them without a password and without sending anything. When they want to use a lab service, they click First time, or forgot your password? on the login page. Keycloak then emails them a link (only if they are a member; the page says the same to everyone).
