After the link, in one go, they choose a password, fill in their name, set up an authenticator app and save their recovery codes, and they are logged in.

  1. Write the members to a file, e.g. members.json. An import doesn't fill anything in by itself, so each user needs a username (the email address) and the realm's default roles (default-roles-lab). Without these roles, users can log in, but the account page shows "Sorry, an unexpected error has occurred" (its requests are refused with 401):

    {
  "users": [
    {"username": "j.doe@example.org", "email": "j.doe@example.org", "enabled": true, "emailVerified": true, "realmRoles": ["default-roles-lab"]},
    {"username": "a.smith@example.org", "email": "a.smith@example.org", "enabled": true, "emailVerified": true, "realmRoles": ["default-roles-lab"]}
  ]
}

  2. In the admin console of lab: Realm settings → Action (top right) → Partial import, choose the file, tick Users, choose Skip for existing users, and click Import. If it fails, the reason is in the log: sudo docker compose logs --since 10m keycloak | grep -E "WARN|ERROR".

  3. Tell the members, e.g.: "Go to , click 'First time, or forgot your password?', and enter your VU email address. You'll get an email with a link to set your lab password (not your VU password). You'll also need an authenticator app on your phone, e.g. Microsoft Authenticator."

    One member at a time: Users → Add user, with the email address (and Email verified on); users added this way get the default roles automatically.

    Members imported without default-roles-lab: import the file again with the roles and Overwrite (this recreates them, so members who already set a password start again with "First time?"), or give one user the role in Users → the user → Role mapping → Assign role (filter by realm roles).

    The texts on the login pages and the email subject ("Sign in with your lab account", "First time, or forgot your password?", "Set your lab password", ...) are in the theme sal-lab (Themes).

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
The login pages, the account console and the emails of all realms use our themes in themes/ (mounted into Keycloak): the lab logo, the blue of the logo, the lab name with a subtitle per realm ("Administration", "Lab account", "Identity provider"), a link to the department page at the bottom, and the texts for lab members. themes/README.md lists which realm uses which theme.

  • Changing a text: edit messages/messages_en.properties of the theme (the keys are Keycloak's own), and restart Keycloak (sudo docker compose restart keycloak): it caches themes. For a quick change without a restart, a realm override (Realm settings → Localization → Realm overrides) takes precedence over the theme.
  • After a Keycloak upgrade: look at the login pages of each realm. The themes change no page templates (only texts, CSS, images, and the footer that Keycloak provides for this), so they normally keep working; a renamed text key falls back to Keycloak's own text.
  • On an existing installation: realms created before the themes keep Keycloak's look. Set them in Realm settings → Themes: master: login theme sal-admin, account theme sal; lab: sal-lab (login and email), account sal; idp: sal-idp, account sal. Also set Realm settings → General → Display name (it is shown in the browser tab): "Societal Analytics Lab administration", "Societal Analytics Lab", "Societal Analytics Lab identity provider". On master, also empty HTML Display name (it holds Keycloak's own logo text).

docs.title: A user lost their second factor
docs.text:
First check who the user is, not by email alone (the inbox may be the problem): e.g. in person, or by a video call. Then, in the admin console of the realm: Users → the user → Credentials, and delete the lost credential (e.g. otp). In lab, the user sets up a new authenticator app (and new recovery codes) at the next login; in idp, they can set up a new one in the account console. For an admin in master, another admin does the same, or see below.

Users who still have a recovery code don't need an admin: they log in with it, and set up a new second factor themselves (see How users log in).

docs.title: Recovering admin access
docs.text:
Recovering admin access (e.g. a lost authenticator app, or no admin left), following the recovery guide. This requires access to the VM, which is the break-glass route. Stop Keycloak and create a temporary admin (you are prompted for a password):

sudo docker compose stop keycloak

sudo docker compose run --rm keycloak bootstrap-admin user --optimized --username recovery-admin

sudo docker compose start keycloak

Log in to the admin console as recovery-admin, fix the problem (e.g. delete the lost OTP credential on the admin's Credentials tab), and delete recovery-admin again.

docs.title: Changing the hostnames
docs.text:
Keycloak reads its hostnames from .env (KC_HOSTNAME, KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN), and Caddy too, so changing them is: point the DNS records to the VM, change .env, and sudo docker compose up -d. Beyond the VM:

  • The master realm stores its admin hostname (its frontend URL) since it was set up. After changing KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN, the admin console keeps sending you to the old one. Change it in the database (fill in the new admin hostname; it should print UPDATE 1), and restart Keycloak:

    sudo docker compose exec postgres psql -U keycloak -d keycloak -c "UPDATE realm_attribute SET value = 'https://<admin hostname>' WHERE name = 'frontendUrl' AND realm_id = (SELECT id FROM realm WHERE name = 'master');"

    sudo docker compose restart keycloak

  • Every app that uses Keycloak has a new issuer URL (https://<hostname>/realms/<realm>): update it everywhere, e.g. the lab login on the lab server. Our own software recognizes users by issuer and user ID, so a new issuer makes existing users look new: check before moving a realm that our servers use (Migration guide).

  • Google and GitHub (idp): update the redirect URI in both developer consoles (https://<hostname>/realms/idp/broker/<google or github>/endpoint).
  • Passkeys only work on the domain they were created on: users sign in with their password and second factor, and register their passkey again.
  • Everyone signs in again, and links in emails sent before the change no longer work.

docs.title: Moving from the old layout (one time)
docs.text:
Until November 2026, the files were in a clone of the documentation repository, in /opt/keycloak/societal-analytics-lab-infra/deploy/keycloak, with a database backup by cron (backup.sh). To move to /opt/keycloak (the database and the realms stay as they are: the volumes belong to the compose project keycloak, whatever its folder):

  1. Make a database backup with the old script, and stop everything (without -v: the volumes stay):

    cd /opt/keycloak/societal-analytics-lab-infra/deploy/keycloak && sudo ./backup.sh

    sudo docker compose down

  2. Move the old folder aside, and create a new, empty one:

    cd / && sudo mv /opt/keycloak /opt/keycloak-old

    sudo mkdir /opt/keycloak && sudo chown keycloak:keycloak /opt/keycloak && sudo chmod 750 /opt/keycloak

  3. Clone the new repository, and copy the local files over:

    sudo -u keycloak git clone https://github.com/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-keycloak.git /opt/keycloak

    sudo cp -p /opt/keycloak-old/societal-analytics-lab-infra/deploy/keycloak/.env /opt/keycloak/.env

    sudo cp -p /opt/keycloak-old/societal-analytics-lab-infra/deploy/keycloak/caddy/admin-access.caddy /opt/keycloak/caddy/admin-access.caddy

  4. Start it, and check that Keycloak works and that the first dump is there:

    cd /opt/keycloak && sudo docker compose up -d --build

    sudo docker compose logs db-backup

  5. Remove the old cron job, and set up the nightly backup (Backups):

    sudo rm -f /etc/cron.d/keycloak-backup

  6. After a week or two, remove /opt/keycloak-old and the old dumps in /var/backups/keycloak.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Likely cause cd /opt/keycloak/... gives Permission denied Your account is not in the keycloak group yet, or you haven't logged in again since adding it. Check with id. permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket The command was run without sudo (see Users and permissions). sudo: ... is not in the sudoers file while logged in as keycloak Docker commands are run from your own admin account, not as keycloak. No certificate, or browser warnings The DNS record doesn't point to the VM yet, or port 80 is blocked. Check sudo docker compose logs caddy. Admin console stays on a loading spinner The frontend URL of master is wrong: check KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN in .env, or, on an installation from before the realm files, step 3. Admin hostname returns 403 while on the VPN Your IP address is not in the ranges in caddy/admin-access.caddy. Check curl -4 https://ifconfig.me on your device. After changing the file, run sudo docker compose exec caddy caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile. A reload of Caddy fails, or Caddy doesn't start after a restart A mistake in caddy/admin-access.caddy: the error message names the file and line. Fix it and reload again (sudo docker compose up -d caddy if Caddy is not running). The admin console of a realm with an exception stays on "Loading", or shows a permission error The exception is missing /resources/* or /admin/serverinfo, or the realm name in the paths is misspelled (see step 4). Requests through Caddy return 502 Bad Gateway Keycloak is still starting, or Caddy doesn't trust Keycloak's internal certificate (e.g. after tls-init renew without restarting Caddy). Run sudo docker compose restart caddy, and check sudo docker compose logs caddy. Requests through Caddy return 403 Forbidden KC_PROXY_HEADERS is not set to xforwarded, so Keycloak's origin checks fail (see the reverse proxy guide). Keycloak doesn't start: Missing in .env: ... A value used in the realm files is not set in .env (see step 7). Keycloak doesn't start on the first start: invalidPasswordMinUpperCaseCharsMessage (or a similar password message) KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD doesn't meet the password policy of master (at least 10 characters, an uppercase letter and a digit). Generate a new one (step 2), and remove the database volume of this failed first start: sudo docker compose down -v (only on a new installation: this deletes all data). Locked out of the admin console after turning on Verify email in master master has no email server, so the verification email never arrives. Don't turn it on (the realm configuration keeps it off). To recover, follow Recovering admin access, but create a service account (bootstrap-admin service --optimized --client-id recovery) instead of a user, because a new user would also have to verify their email. Log in to the admin tool with sudo ./admin-cli.sh login-client recovery (it asks for the secret), turn verification off with sudo ./admin-cli.sh update realms/master -s verifyEmail=false, and delete the recovery client. After renaming a realm, the account console or admin console of that realm doesn't load Keycloak doesn't update the URLs of the built-in clients (account, account-console, security-admin-console): fix their root and redirect URLs by hand, or create the realm again with the new name. admin-cli.sh login <username> fails with Account is not fully set up The account has no email address, while the realm uses email addresses as usernames and has the required action Update email turned on. The realm configuration keeps Update email off in master for this reason; check Authentication → Required actions in master. A login flow asks for OTP twice, or not at all A "Condition - sub-flow executed" refers to a flow name that doesn't exist (e.g. after copying a flow). Run python3 check-realms.py. Users see that an email could not be sent The relay refused or couldn't deliver it. sudo docker compose logs mail-relay shows why, e.g. the cap was reached (Message delivery request rate limit exceeded), a wrong sender address in a realm (Sender address rejected), or a login or TLS problem with the provider. Users see "Please try again later" The email limit per IP address was reached (see Email limits). An app's login fails with invalid_scope ("Invalid scopes") The app requests a scope that idp doesn't offer (only openid, email and profile are offered), e.g. roles or phone. Remove it from the app's settings, or add the scope to that client (Clients → the client → Client scopes) if it really needs it. Creating a client fails with "Invalid Redirect Uri" A redirect URI with http:// or a wildcard, or an empty Valid post logout redirect URIs field: use + there (see step 8). WARN ... configured to build using Bake, but buildx isn't installed Harmless: Compose falls back to the classic build. To remove the warning, install the buildx plugin (sudo apt install docker-buildx-plugin, with Docker from Docker's own repository).

docs.text: The choices behind this setup, and the alternatives that were dropped: Decisions.

docs.title: Installation: lab server
docs.text:
How the lab server is set up: Caddy, the lab login (oauth2-proxy), and how a new service is made reachable. Apps themselves are installed as on every server: Apps on our servers (the system account sal, /opt/<app>, and where data goes). Why it is set up this way: Decisions.

Caddy (in /etc/caddy) is the only thing reachable from outside: it handles HTTPS, and puts the lab login in front of apps that have no login of their own.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text: Two records, both pointing to this server: lab.societal-analytics.nl and *.lab.societal-analytics.nl. New services then need no DNS change. Only the lab's own services may get an address under lab.: see the lab zone.

docs.title: Caddy
docs.text:
Install Caddy from its official apt repository (see Install), not Ubuntu's own caddy package, which is too old. It runs as a service and reads /etc/caddy/Caddyfile. Check caddy version: the snippets below need 2.9 or newer.

HTTPS is automatic: every site with a domain name gets a Let's Encrypt certificate, renewed on its own, as long as its DNS points to this server and ports 80 and 443 are open.

After each change to the Caddyfile, check it, then apply it:

sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile

sudo systemctl reload caddy

Sites keep running during the reload. If the new file has an error, Caddy keeps the old configuration; see why with journalctl -u caddy -n 50.

docs.title: The lab login (oauth2-proxy)
docs.text:
Services without their own login sit behind oauth2-proxy, which sends visitors to the lab's Keycloak (the lab realm). After logging in, they can use every service behind the lab login, until they sign out or are inactive for 2 hours.

In Keycloak (admin console of the lab realm), create the client lab-authwall:

  1. Clients → Create client. Client ID: lab-authwall. Next.
  2. Client authentication: on. Authentication flow: only Standard flow. Next.
  3. Valid redirect URIs: https://lab.societal-analytics.nl/oauth2/callback (the one place every login comes back to; Keycloak doesn't allow a wildcard in the host name). Valid post logout redirect URIs: +. Save.
  4. Advanced tab: Proof Key for Code Exchange Code Challenge Method: S256. Save.
  5. Client scopes tab → lab-authwall-dedicated → Configure a new mapper (or Add mapper → By configuration):
    • Audience: name audience, Included Client Audience lab-authwall, Add to ID token and Add to access token on. oauth2-proxy needs this.
    • Group Membership: name groups, Token Claim Name groups, Full group path off. Only needed for services restricted to a group (Adding a service).
  6. Credentials tab: copy the Client secret.

On the server, create its directory:

sudo mkdir /opt/oauth2-proxy

sudo chown sal:sal /opt/oauth2-proxy && sudo chmod 750 /opt/oauth2-proxy

Create /opt/oauth2-proxy/compose.yml with sudoedit -u sal. oauth2-proxy gets a Docker network of its own, and its port is only published on localhost, for Caddy:

services:
  oauth2-proxy:
    # Pin a release; check https://github.com/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy/releases for a newer one
    image: quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.15.6
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Only for Caddy on this server
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:4180:4180"
    networks: [authwall]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      OAUTH2_PROXY_PROVIDER: keycloak-oidc
      OAUTH2_PROXY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL: https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/lab
      OAUTH2_PROXY_CODE_CHALLENGE_METHOD: S256
      # All members of the lab realm; restrict a service to a group in the Caddyfile (section 2)
      OAUTH2_PROXY_EMAIL_DOMAINS: "*"
      # One login cookie for the lab zone (see [the lab zone](../servers/lab.md#the-lab-zone-everything-under-lab))
      OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_DOMAINS: .lab.societal-analytics.nl
      # Every login comes back here (the redirect URI in Keycloak)
      OAUTH2_PROXY_REDIRECT_URL: https://lab.societal-analytics.nl/oauth2/callback
      # Where users may be sent after logging in or out: the lab's sites (including the website)
      OAUTH2_PROXY_WHITELIST_DOMAINS: .societal-analytics.nl
      # Signing out also ends the Keycloak session (otherwise the next visit logs straight back in)
      OAUTH2_PROXY_BACKEND_LOGOUT_URL: https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/lab/protocol/openid-connect/logout?id_token_hint={id_token}
      # Check the login with Keycloak every 10 minutes: users who signed out, or were inactive
      # longer than Keycloak's idle time (2 hours), have to log in again
      OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_REFRESH: 10m
      # Go straight to the lab login, without oauth2-proxy's own "Sign in" page
      OAUTH2_PROXY_SKIP_PROVIDER_BUTTON: "true"
      OAUTH2_PROXY_REVERSE_PROXY: "true"
      # Requests from the server (Caddy) arrive from the gateway of the network below:
      # only that address may set X-Forwarded-* headers
      OAUTH2_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS: 172.30.255.1/32
      OAUTH2_PROXY_SET_XAUTHREQUEST: "true"
      OAUTH2_PROXY_HTTP_ADDRESS: 0.0.0.0:4180
    # No writes, no extra privileges (the image already runs as a non-root user)
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]

networks:
  # oauth2-proxy alone, with a fixed range, so that the gateway address above is fixed too.
  # Pick a range that no other Docker network on the server uses.
  authwall:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 172.30.255.0/29
          gateway: 172.30.255.1

TODO: until Keycloak has moved to auth.societal-analytics.nl, use its current address in OAUTH2_PROXY_OIDC_ISSUER_URL and OAUTH2_PROXY_BACKEND_LOGOUT_URL.

Its own network keeps oauth2-proxy away from the apps on this server: from inside its container, the services on the server's 127.0.0.1 can't be reached, and no other container can reach oauth2-proxy. (With network_mode: host it could reach every app on the server's localhost, including apps that rely on the lab login.)

Create /opt/oauth2-proxy/.env, also with sudoedit -u sal:

OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID=lab-authwall
OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET=<the client secret from Keycloak>
OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET=<output of: openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -- '+/' '-_'>

Protect the secrets, and start it:

sudo -u sal chmod 600 /opt/oauth2-proxy/.env

cd /opt/oauth2-proxy && sudo docker compose up -d

At the top of /etc/caddy/Caddyfile:

{
    email <admin email address>
}

# The lab login, for services without their own: import authwall { reverse_proxy ... }
(authwall) {
    handle /oauth2/* {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4180 {
            header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
            header_up X-Forwarded-Uri {uri}
        }
    }
    handle {
        forward_auth 127.0.0.1:4180 {
            uri /oauth2/auth
            header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
            copy_headers X-Auth-Request-User X-Auth-Request-Email
            @error status 401
            handle_response @error {
                redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={scheme}://{host}{uri}
            }
        }
        {block}
    }
}

# The same, for a service that only members of one Keycloak group may use:
# import authwall-group <group> { reverse_proxy ... }
(authwall-group) {
    handle /oauth2/* {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:4180 {
            header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
            header_up X-Forwarded-Uri {uri}
        }
    }
    handle {
        forward_auth 127.0.0.1:4180 {
            uri /oauth2/auth?allowed_groups={args[0]}
            header_up X-Real-IP {remote_host}
            copy_headers X-Auth-Request-User X-Auth-Request-Email
            @error status 401
            handle_response @error {
                redir * /oauth2/sign_in?rd={scheme}://{host}{uri}
            }
        }
        {block}
    }
}

# The overview of the lab's services, behind the lab login
lab.societal-analytics.nl {
    import authwall {
        root * /var/www/lab
        templates
        file_server
    }
}

The service receives the user's email address in the header X-Auth-Request-Email. Two separate snippets, because a snippet argument that isn't given stays in the text literally.

docs.title: The overview page
docs.text:
/var/www/lab/index.html (readable by Caddy; e.g. sudo mkdir -p /var/www/lab, then sudoedit /var/www/lab/index.html). Caddy fills in who is signed in (templates). A minimal version:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Lab services</title></head>
<body>
<h1>Lab services</h1>
<p>Signed in as {{.Req.Header.Get "X-Auth-Request-Email"}} ·
<a href="/oauth2/sign_out?rd=https%3A%2F%2Fsocietal-analytics.nl%2F">Sign out</a></p>
<ul>
  <li><a href="https://whisper.lab.societal-analytics.nl/">Whisper</a>: transcription</li>
  <li><a href="https://llm.lab.societal-analytics.nl/">LLM chat</a> (its own login)</li>
</ul>
</body></html>

docs.title: Signing out, and inactivity
docs.text:
What members experience: Signing out, and inactivity. The settings behind it:

  • The 2 hours are the idle time of the lab realm in Keycloak (Realm settings → Sessions → SSO Session Idle); OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_REFRESH makes oauth2-proxy check the session every 10 minutes.
  • To sign out everyone at once (e.g. after a stolen laptop), set a new OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET and restart oauth2-proxy.

docs.title: 2. Adding a service
docs.text:
1. Install the app as described in Apps on our servers, with its port on 127.0.0.1. Its address will be <app>.lab.societal-analytics.nl; DNS needs no change.

  2. Add it to /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.

    • No login of its own: behind the lab login.

      <app>.lab.societal-analytics.nl {
    import authwall {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<port>
    }
}

    • Only for members of one group: create the group in the lab realm (Groups), add the members, and use authwall-group:

      <app>.lab.societal-analytics.nl {
    import authwall-group <group> {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<port>
    }
}

    • Its own login, through Keycloak: create a client for it in the lab realm (Clients → Create client, client authentication on, the app's callback URL as Valid redirect URI), and configure the app's OIDC settings with issuer https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/lab (e.g. Open WebUI):

      <app>.lab.societal-analytics.nl {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:<port>
}

    • For long requests or large uploads, add a transport http { read_timeout 3000s write_timeout 3000s } block inside reverse_proxy, and request_body { max_size 2.5GB } to the site.

    • Add it to the overview page (/var/www/lab/index.html), and reload Caddy.

Moving a service to its address under lab.: keep the old address working for a while with a redirect, e.g. whisper.societal-analytics.nl { redir https://whisper.lab.societal-analytics.nl{uri} }.

Updating or removing an app: see Apps on our servers. After removing one, also remove its block from the Caddyfile and its line from the overview page, and reload Caddy.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Likely cause caddy validate says unrecognized directive: {block} Caddy is older than 2.9 (Ubuntu's own package): install it from Caddy's apt repository (section 1). Keycloak shows "Invalid parameter: redirect_uri" https://lab.societal-analytics.nl/oauth2/callback is not in Valid redirect URIs of lab-authwall, or OAUTH2_PROXY_REDIRECT_URL differs from it. A service behind the lab login returns 502 Caddy can't reach oauth2-proxy (curl -s localhost:4180/ping should print OK), or the service itself. journalctl -u caddy -n 20 says which. "Forbidden" after logging in The service uses authwall-group, and the user is not in that group in the lab realm. A page of oauth2-proxy with a "Sign in" button OAUTH2_PROXY_SKIP_PROVIDER_BUTTON is not set. After signing out, the next visit logs straight back in OAUTH2_PROXY_BACKEND_LOGOUT_URL is missing or wrong, so the Keycloak session wasn't ended. oauth2-proxy doesn't start Check cd /opt/oauth2-proxy && sudo docker compose logs. It needs to reach https://auth.societal-analytics.nl/realms/lab at startup. If the network can't be created, its range is in use: choose another subnet (and gateway, and OAUTH2_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS). oauth2-proxy logs "no --trusted-proxy-ip CIDRs were configured" The setting is missing or misspelled: it is OAUTH2_PROXY_TRUSTED_PROXY_IPS (plural). A change to the Caddyfile has no effect The reload failed: sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, or journalctl -u caddy -n 50.

docs.title: Tested
docs.text:
On a test installation (November 2026), with oauth2-proxy v7.15.6 (built from source, in a container with the settings and network above), Caddy 2.11 with these snippets, and the lab realm of our Keycloak:

  • a first visit to a service goes to the lab login, comes back through the one fixed callback, and ends on the same page; the service receives the user's email address;
  • the login cookie is set for the zone, so a second service needs no login and no redirect; a site outside the zone receives no cookie; a service with its own login under the zone keeps working;
  • the overview page shows who is signed in; signing out there ends the login for all services and the Keycloak session, and goes to the website;
  • with a short idle time: a user who keeps working stays signed in, an inactive user has to log in again, and a 90-second request completes;
  • a service restricted to a group lets members of the group in, and shows "Forbidden" to other lab members;
  • oauth2-proxy sees Caddy's requests from the gateway 172.30.255.1, and ignores forged X-Forwarded-* headers from any other address; it can't reach an app on the server's 127.0.0.1, and another container can't reach it;
  • Keycloak refuses a redirect URI with a wildcard in the host name.

docs.title: Installation: university VMs
docs.text:
How to set up a virtual machine (VM) on VU SciCloud, the VU's research cloud, and secure it before hosting anything on it. This applies to the Keycloak VM and the service VMs. SciCloud is documented by VU Research Data Management (SciCloud, logging in).

Steps 3 to 5 in one script

After creating the VM and logging in as root (steps 1 and 2), setup-vm.sh does steps 3 to 5: your admin user with your SSH keys, the firewall rules, automatic security updates and Docker, and the system account sal for the apps. It can safely run again. Download it, read it, and run it:

cd /tmp && curl -fsSLO https://vu-societal-analytics.github.io/societal-analytics-lab-infra/install/setup-vm.sh

less setup-vm.sh

bash setup-vm.sh <username> --web --ssh-from <VU range 1>,<VU range 2>

--web opens ports 80 and 443 (for a VM that hosts a website or service); --ssh-from <range>,<range> allows SSH only from those ranges, e.g. the VU network (SSH only from the VU network), after checking that your own connection comes from one of them; --caddy also installs Caddy on the VM itself (for service VMs, not for the Keycloak VM). At the end, it asks you to check in a second terminal that you can log in as your new user and use sudo. Only then, turn off root and password logins:

sudo bash /tmp/setup-vm.sh --harden-ssh

The steps below describe what it does, and are the way to do it by hand.

docs.title: 1. Create the VM
docs.text:
Log in to the VM portal at one.labs.vu.nl, from the VU network or the VU VPN.

Public SSH keys. Go to your profile settings (bottom left), then Security, and add your public SSH key(s). They are added to new VMs when they are created.

Create the VM:

  1. Go to Instances → VMs in the left sidebar, and click Create VM (top right).
  2. Choose a template: the latest Ubuntu LTS version (currently Ubuntu 26.04), in one of two variants:
    • (intern): the VM only gets an address inside the VU network. From outside, nothing on it can be reached, whatever its firewall says.
    • (extern): the VM gets a public internet address, e.g. to host a website or service. What can be reached then depends entirely on the VM's own firewall, and the template allows SSH from anywhere: restrict it in step 4.
  3. Settings:
    • A name for the VM.
    • Turn on Instantiate as persistent for a long-running server that stores data (see Persistence).
    • Memory and CPU: what the services on the VM need. For instance, Keycloak needs about 2 GB of memory.
  4. Click Next, and Finish (bottom right).

docs.title: 2. Log in
docs.text:
The VM is listed under Instances; open it to see its IP address. The default user of the Ubuntu templates is root.

From the VU network or the VU VPN:

ssh root@<ip address>

From elsewhere, via the VU SSH gateway (you first log in with your VUnetID and password):

ssh -J <VUnetID>@ssh.data.vu.nl root@<ip address>

If you ever lose access over SSH, the VM's console in the portal still works with a password.

docs.title: 3. Secure SSH logins
docs.text:
Create your own user with administrator rights (sudo), log in with SSH keys only, and turn off logins as root over SSH.

Create a user. Replace username with your own username:

adduser username

usermod -aG sudo username

Give the user your SSH key. The portal added your key(s) for root, so copy those:

mkdir -p /home/username/.ssh && cp /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/username/.ssh/

chown -R username:username /home/username/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/username/.ssh && chmod 600 /home/username/.ssh/authorized_keys

Test before you continue. Keep your current session open, and log in as the new user in a second terminal. Check that sudo works:

ssh username@<ip address>

sudo -v

Only continue when this works, otherwise you can lock yourself out.

Turn off root and password logins over SSH. Put the settings in their own file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. Settings in that folder take precedence over the main configuration file, and on Ubuntu a file in that folder may already turn password logins on, which would silently undo a change to the main file. Files are read in alphabetical order and the first value wins, so the name starts with 00-:

printf 'PermitRootLogin no\nPasswordAuthentication no\nKbdInteractiveAuthentication no\n' | sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf

Check the configuration, and restart SSH (on Ubuntu the service is called ssh):

sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh

Check the settings that are actually in effect. This should show no for all three:

sudo sshd -T | grep -E '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|kbdinteractiveauthentication) '

Then check, in a new terminal, that logging in as root over SSH is refused, and logging in as your own user still works.

docs.title: 4. Firewall
docs.text:
The VMs filter network traffic with iptables, using VU's own setup: the rules are in /etc/iptables-custom, and are loaded with the iptables-custom command. By default, outgoing and incoming traffic may be restricted.

Open the file:

sudo nano /etc/iptables-custom

The file contains VU-specific rules (e.g. access to university services). Leave those in place, and only add the rules you need. Check first whether a rule is already there, to avoid duplicates.

Outgoing web traffic (needed for package updates, git clone and APIs). Under # Filter traffic sent by me:

# Allow outbound web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS) for package managers and APIs
-A OUTBOUND -m state --state NEW -p tcp -m multiport --dports 80,443 -j ACCEPT

Incoming web traffic (if the VM hosts a website or service). Under # Services to the world; with an (extern) template these rules are probably already there:

# Allow inbound web traffic
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

docs.title: SSH only from the VU network
docs.text:
On an (extern) VM, SSH is reachable from the whole internet: anyone can try to log in, or try a flaw in SSH itself. Keys-only logins (step 3) make guessing useless, but SSH still runs code for every connection, before any login. So allow SSH only from the VU network (campus and VPN, which includes the VU SSH gateway), and keep ports 80 and 443 open to everyone. (More options for later: Hardening plan.)

Your VU ranges: the address ranges of the VU network and VPN, as found for the admin restriction of Keycloak (Find your IP ranges). Like the rest of the firewall file, they stay on the VM, not in this documentation.

Replace the general SSH rule. Find it under # Services to the world: a rule with --dport 22 and without -s, e.g. -A INBOUND -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT. Remove it, and add one rule per VU range in its place:

# SSH only from the VU network (campus and VPN, including the VU SSH gateway)
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 22 -s <VU range 1> -j ACCEPT
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 22 -s <VU range 2> -j ACCEPT

Apply it with a safety net: keep your current SSH session open (connected via the VU network or VPN), apply the rules (below), and check that a new login via the VU VPN still works before closing the old one. If something goes wrong, the VM's console in the portal is the way back.

Check from outside: on a phone on mobile data (Wi-Fi off, no VU VPN), ssh <user>@<ip address> (or nc -vz -w 5 <ip address> 22 on a laptop outside the VU) should now time out, while the website still loads.

docs.title: Apply and check
docs.text:
The VMs don't use the standard Ubuntu firewall packages; load the rules with:

sudo iptables-custom

Check the rules that are in effect, for outgoing and incoming traffic:

sudo iptables -S OUTBOUND

sudo iptables -S INBOUND

These rules apply to programs running on the VM itself (e.g. apt, git, curl). They don't apply to Docker containers: see the next section.

docs.title: Docker and the VM firewall
docs.text:
The INBOUND and OUTBOUND rules above don't apply to Docker containers: see Docker warnings.

Reloading the firewall while Docker runs. Check that sudo iptables-custom doesn't remove Docker's own rules. With a container running that publishes ports, the following should show rules for those ports, both before and after sudo iptables-custom:

sudo iptables -t nat -S DOCKER

If the rules are gone after sudo iptables-custom, restart Docker to restore them (running containers restart too):

sudo systemctl restart docker

To verify: on our VM, Docker's chains were still present after sudo iptables-custom, but this still needs to be checked with a container running that publishes ports.

docs.title: 5. Updates and Docker
docs.text:
Security updates. Ubuntu installs security updates automatically with unattended-upgrades. Check that it is installed and enabled:

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades

sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

Some updates (e.g. a new kernel) need a reboot. Ubuntu shows *** System restart required *** when you log in; reboot at a convenient moment. Services started with restart: unless-stopped in Docker Compose come back by themselves.

Docker. Install Docker Engine with the compose plugin, following the official instructions for Ubuntu.

sudo docker compose version

Run Docker with sudo, and don't add users to the docker group: it is effectively root access (see Docker warnings).

docs.title: 6. Installing apps
docs.text: Install apps as described in Apps on our servers: the system account sal, every app in /opt/<app>, and where its data goes. Install Caddy from its official apt repository, as on the lab server (Caddy).

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
To decide whether to use Instantiate as persistent, it helps to know how the portal combines templates, instances and images:

  • Instances are the actual virtual machines.
  • Images are the storage used by a VM: the operating system, swap space, or additional disks.
  • Templates are recipes for VMs. You create an instance by instantiating a template.

Persistence is a property of images, and determines what happens to them when an instance is created and terminated:

Non-persistent image Persistent image When an instance is created The instance gets a disposable copy of the image The instance is linked to the image itself When the instance is terminated The copy is deleted, including all configuration and data The image remains, so the instance can be created again Parallel instances Possible Not possible Use for Temporary machines, e.g. for testing Servers whose configuration or data must not be lost

What "Instantiate as persistent" does: it first makes a copy of the template with persistent copies of its images, and then creates an instance from that copy. If the instance is ever terminated, you can recover it: go to Templates → VMs, find the template with the same name as the instance, and use Instantiate (not Instantiate as persistent).

Persistence is not a backup

A persistent image survives a terminated VM, but not a broken disk, a deleted image, or a mistake on the VM itself. Servers with data still need backups (Backups).

docs.title: Keycloak VM
docs.text: The lab's login service: Keycloak, an open-source identity provider, on a VM of its own in VU SciCloud. The lab server and the lab's services use it for their logins, so they never handle passwords or second factors themselves. Users log in at auth.societal-analytics.nl.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Users((Users))
    Admins((Admins<br/>on the VPN))

    subgraph VM ["Keycloak VM"]
        direction LR
        Caddy["Caddy"]
        KC["Keycloak<br/>realms: master · lab · idp"]
        DB[("PostgreSQL")]
        Relay["Email relay"]
        Caddy -->|internal TLS| KC
        KC --> DB
        KC --> Relay
    end

    Users -->|"auth.societal-analytics.nl<br/>login pages"| Caddy
    Admins -->|"admin hostname<br/>admin consoles"| Caddy
    Relay -->|SMTP| Provider["Email provider"]
  • Two hostnames. auth.societal-analytics.nl is public, but only serves the login pages and what apps need to verify logins; everything else returns 404. The admin consoles, the admin API and the logins of the master realm are only on a separate admin hostname, reachable only from the VPN.
  • Caddy handles HTTPS with certificates from Let's Encrypt, decides which paths are public, and forwards requests to Keycloak over a second TLS connection with an internal certificate that only Caddy trusts. So traffic is encrypted all the way, as Keycloak's reverse proxy guide recommends.
  • PostgreSQL is only reachable by Keycloak, on a network without internet access.
  • The email relay sends all email of Keycloak to the email provider. It is the only place with the provider's password, and it caps the email of the whole installation.

TODO: Keycloak still runs at an older address; it moves to auth.societal-analytics.nl.

docs.title: Three realms
docs.text:
A realm in Keycloak is a separate login: its own users, apps, settings and admins. Users of one realm don't exist in another.

Realm For Login Who can join master Administering Keycloak itself Password and a mandatory second factor Only the administrators lab The lab's own infrastructure: the lab login on the lab server Password and a mandatory second factor Lab members and invited collaborators, added by the lab's admins idp The lab's servers for researchers, such as AmCAT and AnnoTinder Password, Google or GitHub; second factor optional, but required by our servers for sensitive actions Anyone (an account gives no access by itself)
  • master has no email and no external logins, so admin access never depends on an inbox or someone's Google account. Lost access is recovered via the server itself.
  • lab uses institutional email addresses, so there is no Google or GitHub login. Institutional login (via SURF SRAM) may be added later (Decisions).
  • idp is the one login for all of the lab's servers for researchers (below).

All realms show the lab logo and name on their login pages, with a subtitle ("Administration", "Lab account", "Identity provider"), so users know whose login this is; in idp, the consent screen names the app that asks for access.

The realms are set up from realm files in the repository deploy-keycloak (realms/), which Keycloak imports when it starts, for realms that don't exist yet. The files document the configuration, including the login flows, and make it easy to set up the realms again (Realms).

docs.title: How users log in
docs.text:
master lab idp Sign in with Password, or only a passkey Password, or only a passkey Password, only a passkey, Google or GitHub Second factor (2FA) Mandatory Mandatory Optional First time, or forgot password Not possible (no email): another admin, or the VM Email link, the second factor (if any), a new password, and in Same as lab Lost second factor Recovery code, another admin, or the VM Recovery code, or a lab admin Recovery code, or one of our admins

In all realms, the email address is the username. A second factor is an authenticator app (one-time codes, OTP), a passkey or security key, or a recovery code. Tokens contain amr: pwd for a password, mfa for a second factor. Servers that run our software check mfa for sensitive actions (see Two-factor authentication).

Why:

  • Mandatory 2FA in master and lab, because these accounts give access to our infrastructure. Optional in idp, to keep the barrier low for students and collaborators: our servers require mfa for sensitive actions (step-up).
  • A passkey alone counts as two factors: the device, plus a fingerprint, face or PIN to unlock it. Passkeys can't be phished: they only work on our own domain.
  • Email never replaces the second factor. After the email link, users with a second factor must enter it before they can choose a new password, so someone who gets into their inbox can't get in. (Keycloak's default reset logs the user in after the new password without the second factor, and lets them set up a new authenticator app, so an inbox would be enough to take over an account. We changed that.)
  • master has no email and no external logins, so admin access never depends on an inbox or someone's Google account.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
• First time (lab): lab members are added by the lab's admins, without a password (see Adding lab members). The login page says Sign in with your lab account. They click First time, or forgot your password?, enter their email address, and click the link in the email (Set your lab password, valid for 30 minutes). Then, in one go: choose a password, fill in their name, set up an authenticator app, save the recovery codes, and they are logged in. Others get no email (the page says the same to everyone).
  • Password: email address and password, then the second factor if the user has one (Try another way offers the user's other second factors, e.g. a recovery code). In master and lab, users without a second factor set up an authenticator app at their first login, and get recovery codes right after: shown once, to save somewhere safe. (The token of that first login has amr pwd only, because setting up an app doesn't count as using it. A server that requires mfa asks for a code once more.)
  • Passkey: Sign in with Passkey on the login page (or the browser's suggestion in the email field), then the fingerprint, face or PIN. No password and no other factor. Users register a passkey in the account console (Account security → Signing in), which offers it twice. A passkey under Passwordless is for signing in with only the passkey. A passkey under Two-factor authentication is a second factor after the password. Both work.
  • Google or GitHub (idp only): the first time, an account is created with the address from Google or GitHub (Keycloak verifies a GitHub address itself). If an account with that address already exists, Keycloak shows Account already exists: the user links the two by clicking a link sent to the address, or by entering the account's password (and its second factor; after linking it is asked once more, only this first time). After that, users with a second factor are asked for it after Google or GitHub. amr has no pwd for these logins: mfa, or empty.
  • Setting up 2FA later (idp): in the account console (Account security → Signing in). After setting up an authenticator app, Keycloak asks for recovery codes right away. After adding a passkey it doesn't: users who only use passkeys should set up recovery codes there too, or register a second passkey.
  • Forgot password (lab, idp): the same link on the login page, then a link by email (valid for 30 minutes). Users with a second factor enter it first (or a recovery code), then choose a new password, and they are logged in.
  • Remember me (lab): users who tick it stay logged in on that device for up to 30 days (7 days without using it). Without it, the session at Keycloak ends after 30 minutes without use. Sensitive actions in our software still ask for the second factor again (step-up).
  • Lost second factor: log in with a recovery code (Try another way → Recovery Authentication Code; each code works once). Then, in the account console, set up a new authenticator app or passkey, and new recovery codes. Without recovery codes: in lab, a lab admin removes the lost factor after checking who the user is (not by email alone: the inbox may be the problem); in idp, one of our admins does the same; in master, another admin, or the VM (Recovering admin access). How: A user lost their second factor.
  • Time: each page of the login (e.g. setting up the authenticator app, or saving the recovery codes) may take 30 minutes. After that, Keycloak says Your login attempt timed out and the login starts again.

The flows behind these steps: realms/README.md in deploy-keycloak.

docs.title: The idp realm: one login for the lab's servers
docs.text:
idp is the central login of the lab's own servers: our AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers, and other tools later. Users have one account for all of them.

  • Anyone can create an account, with an email address, or with Google or GitHub. An account gives no access by itself: each server decides what a user may do, with roles given to an email address or a user (see Authorization). So students and collaborators sign up themselves when a project gives them access, instead of waiting for an admin.
  • Only the lab's admins add servers (clients), in the admin console (step 8 of the installation guide). A client policy turns on consent and PKCE, and refuses unsafe redirect URIs, so a client can't be created with a mistake. Users always see a consent screen with the server's name before it gets their name and email address.
  • Servers get only what they need: the email address (and whether it is verified), whether the user signed in with 2FA, and the login time; the name only if the server asks for it (the scope profile, which our own software doesn't request). No roles. The consent screen says exactly that, in plain words: "This app will be able to: see your email address; see whether you signed in with two-factor authentication", plus "see your name" for a server that asks for it.
  • Not a service for others. Teams that host our software themselves use their own provider, ideally their institution's (see Authentication provider). The lab's setup, described here, can serve as an example for teams that run their own.

docs.title: More realms
docs.text:
New realms are cheap, and isolated from each other:

  • Isolated realms for the lab's own servers, e.g. one per AmCAT or AnnoTinder server the lab hosts, so that their users don't share accounts with other servers.
  • A realm for a lab member (or their team), with its own admin, who manages it in the admin console of that realm only.

Every new realm can send email through the email relay (host mail-relay, port 587, no login, the lab's sender address). The relay holds the credentials of the email provider: a realm admin can send email through it, but can't read the password or send it to another server, and the relay caps the email of the whole installation.

docs.title: Security in short
docs.text:
• Encrypted all the way: a public certificate between browsers and Caddy, an internal one between Caddy and Keycloak (Map).
  • Only the login paths are public (/realms/, /resources/, /.well-known/, as Keycloak recommends).
  • Admin access only via the VPN: the admin hostname (the admin consoles, the admin API and the master realm) only accepts the VPN's IP ranges, for all realms. A realm for a team outside the university can get an exception for its own admin console. The ranges are only configured on the VM.
  • Mandatory second factor for administrators (master) and lab members (lab); a password reset by email never replaces the second factor (How users log in).
  • The email relay: Keycloak sends all email through it without a password, the relay only accepts our sender address, and it caps the email for the whole installation. Together with a limit per IP address on the requests that send email, this protects the monthly quota of the email provider.
  • Clients with safe defaults: in idp, a client policy turns on consent and PKCE for every client the lab's admins create, and refuses unsafe redirect URIs. It prevents mistakes; it doesn't stop an admin who wants otherwise.
  • Secrets an admin can use but not take: the email provider's password is only in the relay, and the Google and GitHub secrets are stored masked in Keycloak, which refuses to send them to another address without entering them again. This is an extra layer, not a wall: admins can send email and use these logins, and a real admin can always replace the secrets, but not read them out.
  • Brute force detection, a password policy, and login and admin events in all realms, and daily database backups (Backups).

Why it is set up this way: Decisions.

docs.title: Lab server
docs.text: A physical server on VU premises that hosts the lab's services for its members, such as transcription (Whisper) and language models (Ollama). Every service has an address under lab.societal-analytics.nl, and lab.societal-analytics.nl itself is an overview of the services. Which services run here: Hosted services.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Member((Lab member))

    subgraph Server ["Lab server"]
        direction LR
        Caddy["Caddy"]
        Login["Lab login (oauth2-proxy)<br/>sets 🍪 for *.lab"]
        Overview["lab.societal-analytics.nl<br/>overview page"]
        Walled["*.lab.societal-analytics.nl<br/>no own login"]
        Own["*.lab.societal-analytics.nl<br/>own login"]
        Caddy -->|no 🍪| Login
        Caddy -->|🍪| Overview
        Caddy -->|🍪| Walled
        Caddy --> Own
    end

    KC["Keycloak<br/>🔑 lab realm"]

    Member -->|HTTPS| Caddy
    Login -.->|🔑| KC
    Own -.->|🔑| KC
  • Caddy is the only thing reachable from outside. It handles HTTPS (certificates from Let's Encrypt), and sends every request to the right service.
  • The lab login (the AuthWall) protects services without a login of their own, and the overview page. Visitors without its login cookie (🍪) are sent to the lab's login service (the lab realm of Keycloak), so only lab members get in: an account with a password and a mandatory second factor. After that login, the lab login sets the cookie for all of *.lab. A service can be restricted further, to one group of members.
  • Services with their own login (e.g. a chat interface for the language models) are reached directly through Caddy, and log users in through Keycloak's lab realm themselves.
  • The rule: every service under lab. either sits behind the lab login, or has its own login through Keycloak. Never a separate password or token, so lab members have one account, with a second factor, for everything.
  • The services listen only on the server itself (127.0.0.1), so they can't be reached around Caddy. Each one lives in its own directory in /opt, owned by a system account without a login, run with Docker Compose, with its files and database dumps backed up every night, and data with a short retention deleted after a set time (Apps on our servers).

docs.title: The lab zone: everything under lab.
docs.text:
Every service the lab runs for its members gets an address under lab.societal-analytics.nl, such as whisper.lab.societal-analytics.nl, with or without its own login. The DNS has two records for this server, lab and *.lab, so a new service needs no DNS change.

The lab login is one login cookie for the whole zone: after logging in once, members can use every service behind the lab login, and signing out ends the login for all of them.

Only the lab's own services under lab.

The browser sends the login cookie to every address under lab.societal-analytics.nl. Whoever receives it can use it to get into the services behind the lab login, as that user. So only services the lab runs on its own servers may be put under lab., never a site hosted by someone else (an external website host, a SaaS product, a student's own server).

The lab's website (societal-analytics.nl, hosted on GitHub Pages) is outside the zone, and never receives the cookie. Services with their own login under lab. do receive it, but don't use it; they run on the same server, from where they could reach the other services anyway. Why one cookie for the zone, rather than one per service: Decisions.

docs.title: Signing out, and inactivity
docs.text:
• Sign out: the Sign out button on the overview page, or /oauth2/sign_out on any service behind the lab login. It ends the login for all services and the session at Keycloak.
  • Inactivity: members who don't use any service behind the lab login for 2 hours have to log in again. Active members stay signed in: the lab login checks the session with Keycloak every 10 minutes while they work, and a long request (e.g. a large upload) is never cut off.
  • Remember me: members who tick it when they log in stay signed in on that device for up to 7 days without activity.
  • A removed member (or one removed from a group) loses access within 10 minutes. Everyone can be signed out at once, e.g. after a stolen laptop.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: How the server, the lab login and new services are set up: Installation: lab server.

docs.title: Service VMs
docs.text:
Some lab services run on a virtual machine (VM) of their own, on VU SciCloud, rather than on the lab server. That suits services that are open to users outside the lab, or that need their own resources, such as the lab's AmCAT server.

  • Set up like every VM: SSH with keys only, a firewall that only allows HTTPS, and automatic security updates (Installation: university VMs).
  • Apps are installed like on the lab server: in /opt/<app>, with Docker Compose, their files and database dumps backed up every night, and data with a short retention deleted after a set time (Apps on our servers).
  • Caddy on the VM handles HTTPS, in front of the service.
  • Logins go through the lab's login service: the idp realm of Keycloak, where anyone can create an account, and the service decides who gets access.
  • Databases and object storage are on the database server, over an internal, encrypted connection.

Which services run on a VM: Hosted services.
